How does it compare with other routes?

Muniment of title sits between a bare recorded document and a full administration. The table sets out the differences using the code and the Texas State Law Library guides.

Muniment of title next to the other Texas paths for a house
RouteNeeds a willExecutor or administratorWhat gets recorded
Muniment of titleYesNoCourt order and copy of the will, with the county clerk where the property sits
Probate with administrationUsuallyYes, appointed by the courtExecutor's or administrator's deed
Affidavit of heirshipNoNoSworn affidavit with the county clerk, which a third party is not required to accept
Transfer on death deedNoNoDeed recorded before the owner's death, plus an affidavit of death and the death certificate

How soon must someone act?

The will must be filed within four years of the death. The State Law Library adds that a court can sometimes accept a will after that period if the applicant shows an acceptable reason for the delay, though Sec. 257.054 asks the applicant to prove the four years had not run, so waiting is a real risk.

After the will is admitted, the applicant has until the 180th day to file a sworn affidavit with the court clerk stating which terms of the will have been carried out and which have not (Sec. 257.103). The court can waive the report or extend the time. Missing it does not undo title passing under the will.

What does the order do for a house sale?

The order and the will go to the county clerk in the county where the house stands, which builds the chain of title from the owner to the beneficiary. A beneficiary under the will is then entitled to deal with the property as if title were already recorded in the beneficiary's name (Sec. 257.102(b)).

Sec. 257.101 also lets the court add a declaratory judgment to the order, either to interpret an unclear will or to name who takes when the will alone does not say. That judgment is conclusive against an omitted person in a dispute with a good faith buyer who purchased after it was entered.

A few practical steps usually follow:

  • Pay the mortgage or arrange payoff at closing, since the muniment route allows real estate liens to remain.
  • Check the property tax account. Texas taxes attach as a lien on January 1, and the Comptroller's calendar sets the bill date of October 1 and the delinquency date of February 1.
  • Ask the county clerk what the recording fee will be for the order and will. The clerk's manual describes a base fee per page and extra pages priced separately.
Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Who should handle the filing?

The State Law Library says beneficiaries will likely need an attorney to file the application. Some counties also have their own probate court rules and forms, so call the probate clerk in the county where the owner lived before preparing papers.

If the family expects a dispute over the will, or the estate owes unsecured debts, plan for a different path. A muniment order does not fix a will contest and cannot clear debts that fall outside the real estate lien exception.

Which counties and courts are involved?

Two places matter and they are often different. The application goes to the probate court, usually in the county where the owner lived. The order and will are then recorded with the county clerk in the county where the real property sits, which matters when a family house stands in a different county from the owner's last address.

A county clerk also acts as the county recorder and as the clerk who holds probate filings. Under Sec. 257.052, a will filed with the application stays in the clerk's custody unless a court order removes it. A buyer can therefore ask the clerk for certified copies of the order and will to hand to the title company.

For deed recording, the clerk's manual says an instrument conveying real property can be recorded only if it is signed and acknowledged, or sworn before two subscribing witnesses or an authorized officer. When the beneficiary later sells, expect the new deed to need that acknowledgment, even though the muniment order itself already links the chain.

What are the common mistakes with a muniment of title?

Most problems come from the facts that the statute asks the applicant to swear to. Check each before filing.

  • Assuming there are no debts, then finding an unsecured balance that blocks the route.
  • Waiting past the four year period after the death.
  • Leaving out a child born or adopted after the will was signed, which the application must address.
  • Forgetting that a marriage ended after the will was made, another item the application states.
  • Missing the 180 day report, which the court can waive or extend.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use a muniment of title if the house has a mortgage?

Yes. Sec. 257.001 allows it when the only unpaid debts are secured by a lien on real estate. A mortgage fits that description, so the loan can stay in place or be paid off at closing.

Does a muniment of title name an executor?

No. The route is meant for estates that need no administration. Beneficiaries under the will deal with the property directly after the order is entered.

Is there a deadline to apply?

Yes. The applicant must show four years have not passed since the date of death. The State Law Library says a court can sometimes accept a later filing for an acceptable reason, so talk to an attorney quickly.

What do I record to sell the house?

File the court order and a copy of the will with the county clerk in the county where the property sits. That recording links the owner to the beneficiary for the title company.

What if there is no will?

Then muniment of title is not available, because it needs a will. See the heirship affidavit, determination of heirship or administration routes described under Texas intestate succession.

When a Texas resident dies without a will, Estates Code Chapter 201 decides who inherits, and the answer depends on whether there is a spouse, children, parents or siblings and on whether the property is community or separate. This guide summarizes the statute's main rules. It does not cover homestead rights, which Chapter 201 does not address.

Heirs agree to sell?

Who inherits a Texas house when the owner left no will?

Chapter 201 of the Estates Code names the heirs in a fixed order, so the house goes to relatives by a formula, not by what the family expects. The answer turns on whether the owner left a spouse, whether there are children, and whether the house was community property or separate property.

A relative who is entitled to a share becomes an owner the moment the owner dies, but the county records still show the dead person as the owner. Until the heirs are proven in a court order or a recorded affidavit, a title company will usually not insure a sale. That gap between owning and being able to sell is where most Texas families lose time.

What happens when there is a spouse and children?

It depends on which kind of property the house is. The code splits the estate into the community estate and everything else, and each follows its own rule.

For community property, the whole community estate passes to the surviving spouse when the deceased spouse had no descendants, or when every surviving child or grandchild is also a descendant of the surviving spouse (Sec. 201.003). If the owner had a child who is not also the surviving spouse's child, the owner's undivided half of the community estate goes to the owner's descendants instead, and it stays charged with community debts.

For separate property, a surviving spouse with children in the picture takes one third of the personal property and a life estate in one third of the land. The children share the other two thirds of the personal property and hold the remainder interest in the land (Sec. 201.002(b)). Ask a probate attorney who has to sign before a buyer can get clean title when a life estate exists.

How are the shares divided in each situation?

The table below tracks the statute text for the common family patterns. It does not cover every case, and the terms "land" and "personal estate" are the code's own words.

Texas intestate shares by family pattern, from Estates Code 201.001 to 201.003
Family situationWho takes
Spouse survives, community property, all children are also the spouse'sSurviving spouse takes the community estate
Spouse survives, community property, a child from another relationship existsThat child and other descendants take the deceased spouse's undivided half
Spouse and children survive, separate propertySpouse: one third of personal property and a life estate in one third of the land. Children: the rest
Spouse survives, no children, separate property, parent or sibling also survivesSpouse: all personal property and one half of the land. The other half of the land follows the kindred rules
Spouse survives, no children, no parent, no sibling or their descendantsSpouse takes the entire estate
No spouse, children surviveChildren and their descendants
No spouse, no descendants, both parents surviveEqual shares to father and mother

What if the owner had no spouse?

With no surviving spouse, the estate runs down a list of kindred in the order set by Sec. 201.001. Children and their descendants come first and take everything.

  • No descendants, both parents alive: the parents split the estate equally.
  • No descendants, one parent alive: half to that parent and half to the siblings and their descendants, or all to the parent if there are no siblings or sibling descendants.
  • No descendants, no parents: siblings and their descendants.
  • None of those: the estate divides into two halves, one for paternal kindred and one for maternal kindred, working through grandparents and then their descendants.

When a child has died before the owner, that child's own descendants step into the place the child would have filled. The code calls this per capita with representation (Sec. 201.101).

Do adopted children, half siblings and late-born children count?

Adopted children inherit from and through their adoptive parents as if they were born to them, including children a court treats as equitably adopted (Sec. 201.054). The birth parents and their kindred cannot inherit from or through an adopted child.

A child counts as a father's child for inheritance in specific cases: birth within a marriage as described in Family Code Sec. 160.201, a court decree, adoption, or a signed acknowledgment of paternity (Sec. 201.052). Someone who claims to be a biological child can petition the probate court, and the court must find it by clear and convincing evidence. A person must also have been born before the death, or be in gestation at that time, and survive at least 120 hours (Sec. 201.056).

Half siblings take half as much as whole siblings when both kinds inherit together, and a group made up only of half siblings each takes a whole share (Sec. 201.057). These rules can change who has to sign a deed, which is why an overlooked child is the main risk in a quick family sale.

How do heirs prove who they are so the house can be sold?

Texas offers several routes, and the right one depends on the estate. The Texas State Law Library describes the main choices, and each one ends with a document the county clerk can record.

  • Affidavit of heirship: a sworn statement filed with the county clerk. No court reviews it, and no law forces a title company or buyer to accept it.
  • Determination of heirship: a probate court hearing that names the heirs by order. It results in a court order naming the heirs.
  • Small estate affidavit: available only when the estate is within the dollar limit in Estates Code ch. 205, assets are enough to pay debts, and the court approves. A house other than the homestead is a problem here, because the chapter excludes real property except a homestead passing to a spouse or minor children.
  • Administration: the court appoints an administrator, who can later sign a deed.

A buyer who pays value and relies in good faith on a recorded affidavit of heirship that omits a child can still get good title (Sec. 201.053), though the heirs remain liable to the omitted child for the sale proceeds. That rule protects the buyer, not the siblings who signed.

What does selling an inherited house with no will look like?

A typical sale follows a short chain of steps. The order matters because each one supports the next.

  1. Get a certified death certificate and list every relative who could be an heir.
  2. Pick a route to establish title: affidavit, heirship hearing, small estate affidavit where it fits, or administration.
  3. Record the proof with the county clerk in the county where the house sits.
  4. Have every heir, or the court appointed representative, sign the deed or contract.
  5. Settle the property tax bill. Texas property taxes attach as a lien each January 1, so the unpaid balance travels with the house.

If an heir wants to claim the homestead exemption on the inherited home, the appraisal district asks heirs who are not on a recorded deed for an affidavit of ownership interest, the owner's death certificate, a recent utility bill, and any court record citation, as described on the Comptroller exemptions page.

Frequently asked questions

If my parent died without a will in Texas, do I automatically own the house?

If you are an heir under Chapter 201, your interest passes at death, but the record title does not change on its own. You need a recorded affidavit, a court order, or an administrator's deed before a buyer or title company will treat the sale as clean.

Does a surviving spouse always get the house?

No. A spouse takes the whole community estate only when every child is also the spouse's child or there are no descendants. With separate property and children, the spouse gets a life estate in one third of the land and the children hold the remainder.

Can I use an affidavit of heirship to sell an inherited house?

Sometimes. It is a sworn statement filed with the county clerk, and no law makes a third party accept it. Many title companies ask for a court order instead when the family tree is unclear.

What if there is a child nobody listed?

The child can still claim a share. A buyer who relied in good faith on a recorded affidavit keeps good title under Sec. 201.053, but the heirs who sold must answer to that child for the proceeds.

Do siblings inherit if the owner had no spouse or children?

Yes, in the order the statute sets. Both parents alive take equal shares. If neither parent is alive, the siblings and their descendants take the whole estate.

In Texas a will does not prove title to property until it is admitted to probate (Estates Code Sec. 256.001), and it generally must be offered within four years of the testator's death. This guide covers what Chapter 256 says about the application, proof, the order and later challenges.

Estate house still waiting?

What does probate mean for a Texas family that wants to sell the house?

Probate is the court procedure that turns a death into a clear owner on paper. A buyer's title company wants that paper before it insures anything, so a Texas house tied to an estate generally waits on one of several routes before it can change hands.

Texas has no single statewide probate office. Each filing lands in a particular county, so the practical work is local even though the rules come from state law. The Texas State Law Library publishes plain-language guides on each route, and the Texas courts publish a manual for county clerks that shows what the clerk's office will accept.

Think of the process as three questions. Was there a will? Does the estate owe anything beyond a mortgage? Do all the heirs agree? The answers point to the route in the table further down.

How long can an heir wait before a will must be offered to the court?

The usual limit is four years after the person dies, and the court may take a later application for an acceptable reason. The State Law Library guide on probating a will is the source for that window.

Sellers should care about the date because a signed will sitting in a drawer gives nobody authority over the house. If a relative died several years ago and nobody opened an estate, count the years first. A probate attorney, or the clerk of the probate court in the county of the person's last home, can say what the file shows.

  • A formal will is in writing, signed, and witnessed by two people.
  • A will in the maker's own handwriting needs no witnesses.
  • The application normally goes to the probate court for the county of the person's last residence.

Which Texas probate routes fit a house, and what does each one require?

The route depends on whether a will exists, what the estate owes and whether the heirs agree. The table pulls together the routes described in the State Law Library guides and the county clerk manual.

Routes to clear title on an estate house, summarized from Texas State Law Library guides
RouteTypical situationPaper a buyer will see
Full administrationWill exists and a representative must collect assets and pay debtsCourt order, then an executor's or administrator's deed
Muniment of titleWill exists, nothing owed except real estate liens, no administration neededCourt order plus the will, filed with the clerk for the land's county
Small estate affidavitNo will, $75,000 or less in assets excluding homestead and exempt propertyCourt-approved affidavit; the homestead copy is recorded
Heirship affidavitFamily swears to who the heirs areSworn statement filed with the clerk
Transfer on death deedOwner signed and recorded one while aliveRecorded affidavit of death and death certificate

No route is quick by default. The best one is whichever the estate actually qualifies for.

When does a muniment of title make sense for an estate house?

It suits a family with a valid will, no creditors beyond liens on real estate, and no need for a personal representative to run the estate. The judge admits the will and issues an order, and both documents are filed in the land records of the house's county.

For a seller this is often the tidiest result, because a title company can read the recorded order and see who took the house under the will. A surprise debt from a credit card or medical bill can push the estate into full administration, so ask the family attorney to confirm that nothing else is owed.

Who can use a small estate affidavit, and who cannot?

Only estates with no will and no administration underway, assets under the $75,000 line (homestead and exempt property left out), enough assets to cover the debts and agreement among every heir. Estates Code chapter 205 sets these terms, and the State Law Library repeats them.

Two limits catch families off guard. The estate cannot hold land other than a homestead that passes to a spouse or minor children, and the court must approve the affidavit. The clerk manual adds that two disinterested witnesses swear to it, that 30 days must pass after the death and that no petition for a personal representative may be pending or granted.

  • A second house or rental lot usually rules this route out.
  • One heir who objects stops it.
  • Ask the clerk which forms the local court expects.

Can a sworn heirship statement or a transfer on death deed stand in for probate?

Sometimes, with a catch for each. The heirship statement is sworn and filed with the clerk without any judge reviewing it, and nothing obliges a buyer, lender or title company to rely on it.

The transfer on death deed is different because the owner prepared it before dying. Per the State Law Library, it moves land outside probate, can be revoked by the owner and has to reach the land records before the owner dies. Afterward the heirs record an affidavit of death with the death certificate. The related Lady Bird deed, an enhanced life estate, lets the owner sell or mortgage without asking the people named to inherit.

When neither exists, the court options in the guide are a determination of heirship or an order of no administration.

Who signs the deed to the buyer once the estate is ready to sell?

The signer follows the route. A court-appointed executor or administrator signs after full administration. After a muniment, the heirs named in the will take title and sign. After such a deed, the beneficiary who recorded the affidavit signs as owner.

The clerk cannot add names to an older deed, so the proof of how title moved has to sit in the land records before the sale closes. The deed itself needs a notary or similar officer to witness the signature. Ask the clerk for the current recording charges, which the 2023 clerk manual shows as a per-page schedule with local add-ons.

Does the tax bill or homestead exemption change when an owner dies?

Property tax keeps running. Each year's tax lien arises at the start of the year, and the person who owned the house then is the one liable, per the Comptroller's deadlines page.

Texas ended its inheritance tax with Senate Bill 752, effective September 1, 2015. Heirs living in the house may keep claiming a homestead exemption. Heirs missing from a recorded deed hand the appraisal district a sworn ownership statement, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation. A spouse who is 55 or older may in some cases carry over the over-65 exemption. The appraisal district has the current forms.

What should heirs gather before calling a buyer?

Gather the paper that proves authority, then list what the sale must pay off. Missing authority is the most common reason an inherited sale stalls.

  • The will, if one exists, and the date of death.
  • The case number from the probate court, or confirmation that none is open.
  • A search of the land records for a transfer on death deed.
  • Mortgage and tax balances, since both are settled from the proceeds.
  • A decision among heirs about who signs.

A title company can say what it needs before closing, and an attorney can confirm which route fits the estate.

Frequently asked questions

What is the time limit to probate a will in Texas?

Four years after the death, as a general rule. A court can accept an application filed later when the applicant explains the delay acceptably.

Can heirs sell an estate house before the court finishes?

Usually not to a buyer who needs title insurance. The buyer will want an executor's deed, muniment order or approved affidavit on record first.

What is the asset ceiling for a Texas small estate affidavit?

$75,000, with the homestead and exempt items left out of the count. The estate must also have no will, no open administration and unanimous heirs.

Is there a Texas inheritance tax today?

No. Senate Bill 752 repealed it as of September 1, 2015, though property tax stays due.

Which office records probate documents for a house?

The county clerk for the county holding the house. The clerk records the deed or order once it carries a proper signature and notarization.

In Texas, neither spouse can sell, convey or encumber the homestead without the other spouse's signature, whether the homestead is separate or community property. That rule is in Family Code Sec. 5.001. The code also sets who manages community and separate property and has a court process for selling when a spouse has disappeared or abandoned the home.

Spouse not on board, or missing?
Tell us about the situation. We buy as-is and work with a title company on what a sale needs.

Can one spouse sell the family home in Texas?

Not alone, if the house is the homestead. Family Code Sec. 5.001 says that whether the homestead is one spouse's separate property or community property, neither spouse may sell, convey or encumber it without the other spouse joining, unless the chapter or other law provides an exception.

That rule trips up sellers who hold title in one name. A deed signed by the titled spouse alone may leave the buyer without clear title, and a title company will ask about marital status before it commits to insure. A house that is not the homestead, such as a rental the couple owns, follows the management rules in Chapter 3 instead.

What counts as community property versus separate property?

Chapter 3 of the Family Code sorts property by when and how it was acquired. The sorting matters because it controls who may sign and who shares in the proceeds.

  • Separate property: what a spouse owned or claimed before marriage, what a spouse received during marriage by gift, devise or descent, and personal injury recoveries other than lost earning capacity (Sec. 3.001).
  • Community property: everything else either spouse acquired during marriage (Sec. 3.002).
  • Presumption: property possessed by either spouse during or at the end of the marriage is presumed community, and proving it separate takes clear and convincing evidence (Sec. 3.003).

A house bought during the marriage with wages is community even when only one name is on the deed. A house one spouse inherited is separate, though the other spouse may still have homestead rights in it if the couple lives there.

Who manages the property when a house is not the homestead?

Each spouse has sole management of their own separate property, per Sec. 3.101. For community property, Sec. 3.102 gives each spouse sole control of the community property that spouse would have owned if single, such as personal earnings and revenue from separate property. Anything else is under joint management unless the spouses agree otherwise by written power of attorney or another agreement.

Section 3.104 protects outsiders. During marriage, property held in one spouse's name is presumed to be under that spouse's sole control, and a third person who deals with that spouse can rely on it if they are not part of a fraud and have no notice of a lack of authority. That presumption does not override the homestead rule, which is why an investor buying a homestead still needs both signatures.

What if the other spouse is missing, has left, or cannot sign?

The Family Code has two court tracks, and both start with a sworn petition. Subchapter B of Chapter 5 covers the homestead itself, and Subchapter D of Chapter 3 covers other community property.

Court options when a spouse cannot join the sale
SituationStatuteWhat the law provides
Spouse declared incapacitated by a guardianship courtSec. 5.002 and 5.003Competent spouse may sell without the other's joinder
Spouse disappeared, abandoned the home, or permanently separatedSec. 5.101 and 5.102Sworn petition to sell without joinder
Spouse reported prisoner of war or missing on public serviceSec. 5.101(4) and 5.102(4)Petition allowed, with a court-appointed attorney for the respondent
Community property other than the homesteadSec. 3.301Petition to manage and dispose of described community property

Source: Family Code ch. 5 and ch. 3.

How long does the court process take to start, and what can the judge order?

A petitioning spouse cannot file at once. Section 5.103 sets the earliest filing at the 60th day after the disappearance, abandonment or permanent separation, and at six months after a spouse is reported as a prisoner of war or missing on public service. The petition goes to a court in a county where any part of the property is located.

The judge may appoint an attorney for the respondent, and must do so when the respondent is reported as a prisoner of war or missing. If the spouse's residence is unknown, citation by publication runs for two consecutive weeks before the hearing under Sec. 3.305.

Under Sec. 5.106 and 3.306, the court may attach conditions to protect the other spouse, require a bond, and order some or all sale proceeds paid into the court registry. An order that affects real property is not constructive notice to a good faith purchaser unless it is recorded in the deed records of the county where the land sits (Sec. 3.308).

What happens to the house when a spouse dies?

Estates Code ch. 201 governs a death without a will. The community estate passes to the surviving spouse when the decedent left no descendants, or when all surviving children are also the spouse's children. If a child from another relationship survives, the decedent's undivided one-half interest in the community passes to that child line, charged with community debts.

Separate property follows other rules. With children, the surviving spouse takes a life estate in one-third of the land. With no children, the spouse takes half of the land. The Texas Department of Insurance also notes that a title policy generally does not cover homestead, community property or survivorship rights of a policyholder's spouse, so a clean spousal signature or court order matters to the buyer.

Can a written agreement change who owns what?

Yes. Sec. 3.410 recognizes premarital and marital property agreements that meet Chapter 4 requirements, and says such an agreement can waive, release, assign or partition reimbursement claims. Sec. 3.004 separately allows a signed and acknowledged schedule of a spouse's separate property to be recorded in the deed records.

The recording matters for real estate. A schedule of separate real property is not constructive notice to a good faith purchaser or an unaware creditor unless it is acknowledged and recorded in the deed records of the county where the land sits. Anyone relying on such an agreement to sell without a spouse should talk with a Texas family law attorney first, because the homestead rule in Sec. 5.001 still applies to the house the couple lives in.

How do reimbursement claims affect a sale?

One marital estate can owe another when it paid for the other's debts or improvements. Under Sec. 3.404 a reimbursement claim does not create an ownership interest, but it is a claim against the benefited estate that matures on divorce or death. On divorce or death, a court may impose an equitable lien on the benefited property under Sec. 3.406.

This often arises when community wages paid down a mortgage on a house one spouse owned before marriage. Raise the point with your closing attorney before listing, since a lien claim can show up in a divorce decree and a recorded document.

Frequently asked questions

Do both spouses have to sign a deed to sell a Texas homestead?

Yes, in general. Family Code Sec. 5.001 says neither spouse may sell, convey or encumber the homestead without the other spouse joining, whether it is separate or community property, except where the code provides otherwise.

What if my spouse left and I cannot find them?

Sec. 5.102 lets you file a sworn petition to sell a community homestead without joinder when the spouse has disappeared, permanently abandoned the home, or the spouses are permanently separated. You cannot file until the 60th day after the event.

Is a house I bought before marriage community property?

No, it is separate property under Sec. 3.001. If the couple makes it their homestead, the spouse's signature is still required for a sale under Sec. 5.001 unless an exception applies.

Can a spouse sell if the other has dementia?

If a guardianship court has declared the other spouse incapacitated, Sec. 5.002 and 5.003 let the competent spouse sell without joinder. Without that judicial declaration, a power of attorney or court order is the usual route.

Does a divorce decree change who can sell?

It can. A decree usually awards the house to one spouse and may order a sale. Title companies ask for a recorded decree or deed so the buyer can see who holds title, and a Sec. 3.406 lien may also appear.

What is a deed of trust in Texas?

A deed of trust is the document most Texas homeowners sign to secure a mortgage loan, and it usually gives the lender a power of sale. If the borrower defaults, the lender can sell the home at a public auction without going to court first.

The loan itself is the promissory note. The deed of trust is the lien paper that ties the house to that note. When the note is paid off, the lender releases the lien, and that release is lodged in the clerk's office so the public record shows the house is free of that debt.

Texas law recognizes three routes to foreclose. The State Law Library describes them this way:

  • Judicial foreclosure, which goes through a lawsuit and is uncommon in Texas.
  • Nonjudicial foreclosure, which relies on the power of sale in the deed of trust and is governed by Property Code section 51.002.
  • Expedited foreclosure, which needs a court order and is the required route for home equity loans, reverse mortgages and some owners' association assessment liens.

How does nonjudicial foreclosure work under a deed of trust?

It works through a series of written notices followed by an auction, with no judge deciding whether the sale goes ahead. Because no court is involved, the notice deadlines in the statute carry most of the weight for the borrower.

For most home loans, a federal rule bars a servicer from starting foreclosure until the loan is more than 120 days delinquent. After that, the servicer sends a notice of default. The borrower can bring the loan current by paying the past-due amount within 20 days of receiving that notice, under section 51.002(d).

If the default is not cured, the servicer then sends a notice of sale. It must go out three weeks or more ahead of the auction, with a copy on the courthouse door and another lodged with the clerk. Read each letter the day it arrives, because the dates printed on it set the schedule.

When and where is a Texas deed of trust foreclosure sale held?

Auctions are open to the public and happen on a month's first Tuesday during daytime hours. January 1 and July 4 are the exceptions, when the first Wednesday takes over, based on informal Attorney General guidance.

Start time is whatever the notice says, with a three-hour outer limit. Each commissioners court names the sales area and records it, so the clerk can tell you where bidding will happen.

How do the note and the deed of trust differ for a seller?

The note is the promise to repay, and the deed of trust is the security that lets the lender enforce it against the house. A seller usually needs a payoff statement from the servicer, and a title company will confirm that the lien is released when the loan is paid at closing.

Sellers whose house is in default often ask what a buyer can do. A buyer who pays off the loan before the auction gets a house whose lien is cleared in the record. After an auction, the buyer instead receives a trustee's deed recorded by the county clerk.

The same clerk records every instrument, so a title search shows each deed of trust, release and foreclosure notice in order. Reading that chain is the quickest way to see who holds a lien on the home and whether any paper is missing.

What happens after a deed of trust sale?

The winning bidder takes the property, and the former owner may still owe money. The lender can file a deficiency suit if the sale price fell short of the debt, but the clock is two years from the sale date. A borrower can ask the court to credit the home's fair market value against what is claimed.

If the sale brings in more than the debt, the extra money goes first to junior lienholders and then to the former owner. Texas does not give an automatic right to buy the house back after this kind of sale. Redemption rights exist only for certain situations, such as particular tax liens and owners' association assessment liens.

A buyer who finds the former owner still living in the house may need to file an eviction case to get possession. The notice and court steps for that are covered on the eviction pages of this site.

How is a deed of trust recorded and released with the county clerk?

Recording belongs to the county clerk, who serves as county recorder for deed records. A deed of trust, its release, and a trustee's deed after a sale all land in that same record.

To be recorded, an instrument that conveys real property needs a signature plus an acknowledgment, or an oath before two subscribing witnesses or an officer authorized to take acknowledgments, under Property Code section 12.001(b). The 2023 county clerk manual lists the standard fees:

  • A $5.00 charge for page one, then $4.00 for every added page or attachment.
  • $0.25 for each name over five that must be indexed.
  • A records management and preservation fee of no more than $10 and a records archive fee of no more than $10.
  • A records technology and infrastructure fee of $2.00.

Fees can change, so ask the county clerk for the current schedule before you file. After a loan is paid, confirm that the release of the deed of trust shows up in the clerk's index.

What can a Texas homeowner do when a deed of trust loan is in default?

The most direct option is to act inside the 20-day reinstatement window and ask the servicer for the exact payoff figure needed to cure. Missing that window does not end every option, but the later steps are tied to the sale calendar.

These are the main paths people weigh:

  • Bring the loan current with a reinstatement payment.
  • Ask the servicer about a repayment plan or loan modification before the sale date.
  • Sell the house before the first Tuesday sale so the proceeds pay off the lender and any remaining equity stays with you.
  • Speak with a Texas attorney or a legal aid office about your specific notice.

A sale before the auction date generally leaves a cleaner record than a foreclosure, because the lien is paid and released rather than enforced. Gather the notice of default, the notice of sale, and your loan statements first, since any buyer or lender will ask for them.

Frequently asked questions

Does Texas require a court order to foreclose on a deed of trust?

Usually no. Nonjudicial foreclosure under the power of sale in the deed of trust does not need a court order. Home equity loans, reverse mortgages and certain owners' association assessment liens need an expedited court order instead.

What is the cure period after a notice of default?

Twenty days from receipt. Paying the overdue amount in that span reinstates the loan under Property Code section 51.002(d). Ask the servicer for a written reinstatement figure so the amount is exact.

Can a Texas foreclosure sale happen on any day?

No. Sales are set for a month's first Tuesday, or the first Wednesday when January 1 or July 4 is that Tuesday. The notice gives a start time, and bidding has to begin within three hours of it.

Can I still owe money after the house is sold at auction?

Yes, possibly. A deficiency suit is allowed for two years after the sale, and you may ask for a credit based on the home's fair market value. Surplus sale money goes to junior liens first and then to the former owner.

Where do I find recorded deeds of trust and releases in Texas?

Search the clerk's records for the property's home county. The clerk records deeds of trust, releases, trustee's deeds and foreclosure sale notices, and charges the filing fees set by statute.

What is the Texas foreclosure process?

Judicial foreclosure exists but is rare. An expedited court order is the required path for home equity loans, reverse mortgages and owners' association assessment liens. Which route applies depends on the loan type, so check your loan papers.

When can a lender start foreclosing on a Texas home?

For most home loans, federal rules bar a servicer from starting foreclosure until the loan is over 120 days delinquent. That gives the borrower a stretch of time to talk to the servicer before any formal notice arrives.

Texas also limits how long a lender has to act. Civil Practice and Remedies Code section 16.035 sets a four-year limitations period on foreclosure actions, with exceptions. If you received an old default notice, ask an attorney whether that period is relevant.

What notices does a Texas borrower receive?

Two notices matter most: the notice of default and the notice of sale. Each starts a deadline.

  • Notice of default: the borrower can reinstate by paying the past-due amount within 20 days of receiving it, under Property Code section 51.002(d).
  • Notice of sale: sent once the 20 days run out, with 21 days or more left before the auction.
  • Posting and filing: the notice of sale goes on the courthouse door and with the county clerk, which charges $2.00 per notice according to the 2023 clerk manual.

The foreclosing lender is paid first from the bid. Excess funds go to junior liens and then to the former owner.

Does a Texas homeowner have a right to redeem after foreclosure?

The commissioners court is the body that designates where in the county sales are held, so the clerk is the person to ask when you cannot tell where an auction will take place.   • Call or visit the clerk where the house is located, not where you live.

  • The notice of sale and the date printed on it.
  • Recent loan statements and any letters from the servicer.
  • Proof of homestead use if you live in the house.

If property taxes are behind, note that each year's tax lien arises on the first of January, and a lender may pay the taxes and add them to your balance. Ask your servicer to confirm how taxes are being handled.

Why do the dates on the notices matter so much?

Every protection a borrower has in Texas is attached to a date printed on a paper. The cure period begins on receipt of the default letter, and the auction cannot be held until the sale letter has aged long enough. Write each date on a calendar the day the mail arrives.

If a letter looks wrong, for example a sale date that is not a Tuesday, or a county that does not match the property, raise it with the servicer in writing and consult an attorney quickly. Small defects in timing or place can matter, and the window to act closes at the auction.

At least 21 days. Posting on the courthouse door and a filing with the clerk are both required.

Can the lender still sue me after the auction?

The Texas Real Estate Commission's resale contract, Form 20-19, splits them: the seller pays lien releases, tax certificates, deed preparation and half the escrow fee, and the buyer pays loan costs and the other half of the escrow fee. Who pays closing costs when a Texas house sells?

The sales contract decides, and in most resale deals the contract is a standard form from the Texas Real Estate Commission. TREC lists its One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Form 20-19, with an effective date of July 1, 2026, and describes it as the most frequently used contract for single-family homes, duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes.

The form does not cover condominiums, new homes sold by a builder, or farm and ranch property. Those use other TREC forms, so a seller of one of those property types should check which contract applies before negotiating. Ask your agent or title company to walk you through the cost paragraphs of whichever form is used, since individual lines can be changed by negotiation.

What does a Texas seller typically see on the closing statement?

Expect charges tied to clearing title and settling the year's taxes, plus anything you agreed to cover in the contract. The items below come from the official pages that describe how Texas closings work.

  • Payoff of any mortgage or other lien, so the lienholder's claim is released at funding.
  • Property taxes for your share of the year, because the lien attaches on January 1 and the buyer cannot get clear title with delinquent taxes outstanding.
  • The owner's title policy premium, if the contract assigns it to you.
  • Escrow, tax certificate and delivery charges, which the Texas Department of Insurance says many title companies add.
  • Recording charges for any release or curative document you must file.
  • Seller concessions, if you agreed to contribute toward the buyer's costs.

Lenders must give buyers a Closing Disclosure three business days before closing, according to the CFPB. A seller can ask the title company for a draft settlement statement in the same window.

Who pays for the owner's title policy in Texas?

The buyer and seller may negotiate it. The Texas Department of Insurance says the premium is paid once at closing, and that the parties can agree on who bears it.

The amount is not negotiable with the title company. TDI says Texas title rates are regulated and that every title company charges the same premium for a given policy. As printed on its FAQ, the basic premium is $496 for a $50,000 property and $832 for a $100,000 property. That page also notes that the premium covers the title search, examination and closing service, so you are not billed separately for those pieces.

Title insurance is not required by Texas law, per TDI, though a lender will require a loan policy. TDI also warns that you may pick any title company, and that RESPA bars a seller from conditioning the sale on a particular insurer.

What should a seller do before closing day to avoid surprises?

Gather the paperwork and questions early, because a Texas closing moves quickly once a contract is signed.

  • Confirm in writing who pays the owner's policy premium and which escrow fees fall to you.
  • Pull the current tax bill and note the year's due dates.
  • If the property is held by a married couple, confirm both spouses will sign.

Those steps cost nothing and tend to catch errors while there is still time to fix them.

What is the difference between a title commitment and a title policy?

Per TDI, the commitment arrives before closing and the policy is issued afterward. The commitment says the company is willing to insure the buyer on stated conditions, including any problems the seller must fix. It lists potential issues, exclusions and exceptions, and it does not promise that no problem exists.

For a seller, the commitment is the early warning. It can reveal a lien, an unpaid judgment or a gap in the chain of ownership while there is still time to cure it. TDI's list of title defects includes forged or improperly witnessed documents, unrecorded easements, liens for unpaid taxes or association charges, and claims from missing heirs.

Read the commitment as soon as the buyer's title company produces it, and ask the escrow officer which items you are expected to clear. A seller who clears them quickly avoids a delayed funding date.

What other charges can a title company add?

TDI tells consumers that escrow fees differ between companies, and it names tax certificates, escrow, recording and delivery as common add-ons beyond the premium. You may review the closing papers ahead of time and bring a lawyer.

How do property taxes interact with the sale?

Bills go out around October 1, and the Comptroller says delinquency begins February 1 for most. Penalty and interest accrue from there, and the Comptroller's payment page prints the full schedule.

Because that year's lien attaches on January 1, a closing early in the year can find the prior bill still open. The Comptroller adds that whoever owned on that January date remains liable, even after selling. So request the tax certificate at the start of the process and make sure the payoff covers any unpaid year.

Buyers who take title after January 1 may be able to claim the school homestead exemption for the rest of that year if the seller never held it. Mention that to your buyer.

Is there a Texas transfer tax on the deed?

The sources cited here list recording fees but no state transfer tax. A county clerk records instruments for the county in which the land lies, and the instrument has to be acknowledged or sworn before an authorized officer.

They can. The IRS measures gain from your adjusted basis and amount realized, and the Topic 701 exclusion applies to what remains. Publication 523 is the place to learn which selling expenses count. Texas imposes no state income tax, according to the Comptroller, so the question is federal only.

Keep the final settlement statement. The CFPB also notes that some lines are credits and others charges, so read each line, including seller-paid items.

Can I negotiate the title insurance premium in Texas?

No. TDI says the premium is regulated and every title company charges the same amount for a policy. What you can negotiate with the buyer is who pays it, and you can compare escrow and other fees between companies.

Is title insurance required to sell a Texas home?

Texas does not require it, per TDI. A buyer's lender will require a loan policy, and buyers often purchase an owner's policy as well. The contract says who pays for it.

What are the recording fees for a Texas deed?

The 2023 clerk manual prints $5.00 for page one and $4.00 for later pages, plus capped records fees. Counties differ on some charges, so get today's schedule from the clerk.

Will I owe property tax at closing if I sell in the spring?

Possibly. The lien attaches each January 1 and most bills are delinquent after January 31, so the prior year must be paid and the current year divided between you and the buyer. The settlement statement shows the split.

Our offer is as-is, with no inspection negotiations or agent commissions. Tell us about the property.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

The Texas Real Estate Commission's One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Form 20-19, effective July 1, 2026, leaves the option period length as a blank for the parties to fill in. During that period the buyer can terminate for any reason by giving notice by 5:00 p.m. local time. This guide walks through the option period, the Seller's Disclosure Notice, title deadlines and default remedies as the form states them.

Prefer a simple as-is sale?
No inspection negotiations, no repair requests and no agent commission. Get a written cash offer.

What is the option period in a Texas home sale contract?

It is a window in which a buyer who paid an agreed option fee can end the contract for any reason by giving the seller written notice. TREC's FAQ describes it that way and adds that the termination option is a negotiable term, so a buyer does not have to pay for one.

Buyers typically use the days to inspect the house and negotiate repairs through an amendment, or to walk away. For a seller, the period is the stretch in which the deal can end without the buyer giving a reason, so the numbers written into the contract matter.

Which TREC contract form is used for a resale in 2026?

The One to Four Family Residential Contract (Resale), Form 20-19, with an effective date of July 1, 2026. TREC calls it the most frequently used contract form, for the resale of a single family home, duplex, triplex or fourplex.

TREC says it is not for condominium sales, new homes sold by a builder, or farm and ranch property, and TREC publishes separate forms for those. The Commission's contracts page lists many addenda alongside it, including a third party financing addendum, a seller financing addendum, a short sale addendum and a back-up contract addendum.

How do the option fee and earnest money work?

The buyer delivers earnest money and the option fee to the escrow agent. TREC's FAQ quotes paragraph 5A of an earlier edition of the form as requiring delivery within three days of the effective date, and quotes paragraph 5D for the consequence: if no option fee amount is stated or the buyer fails to deliver it on time, the buyer has no unrestricted right to terminate under that paragraph.

Because the FAQ quotes an earlier edition, read the paragraph numbers and day counts in the current 20-19 itself, or ask your agent or title company to point them out. TREC counts days from the effective date, with the first day being the next day, and each day is a calendar day.

  • Option fee: set by the parties, paid to the seller for the termination right.
  • Earnest money: held by the escrow agent.
  • Option days: a negotiated number written into the contract.
  • Notice: written, delivered to the other side.

How are days counted when a contract has deadlines?

TREC's FAQ says the count starts with the effective date, which is the date of final signature, and the first day of any period is the day after. Every day is a calendar day, so weekends and holidays count. A seller who signs on a Friday should see that the next day is day one, and should ask the agent to mark the end date on a calendar.

Notices tied to a deadline should be sent in the manner the contract's notice paragraph requires, and a missed deadline can change what a party may do. Because TREC does not decide whether a contract is valid or which party wins a dispute, keep a dated copy of every notice sent or received.

What if the buyer never paid earnest money?

TREC says its forms require the buyer to deliver earnest money to the escrow agent, and if the buyer does not deliver it on time, the seller may terminate or exercise remedies under the contract's default paragraph. TREC adds that it has no jurisdiction to decide who is entitled to earnest money.

If a dispute over earnest money arises, TREC points people to a private attorney, and says it has no authority over title companies. It can take complaints about a license holder who fails to deposit earnest money as the contract requires.

What must a Texas seller disclose?

Texas sellers of previously occupied single family homes complete the Seller's Disclosure Notice, TREC Form 55-1, which carries an effective date of May 28, 2026 on TREC's page. TREC says the form covers information required by Section 5.008 of the Property Code about material facts and the physical condition of the property, and applies with a contract entered into on or after September 1, 2023.

Give the notice completely and accurately, and ask your agent how to answer any question about repairs or known defects. TREC's FAQ warns that a mistake in completing a form can lead to financial loss or an unenforceable contract.

How do repair terms and the option period fit together?

TREC's FAQ says a buyer should check the box for specific repairs only if particular repairs are known when the contract is signed. Otherwise the buyer checks the as-is box, and most buyers then pay for an option period to inspect and negotiate.

Repair paths described in TREC's FAQ
SituationWhat TREC says to do
Specific repairs known at signingUse the specific-repairs choice and list them
No known repairsUse the as-is choice
Repairs found by inspectionAmend the contract, or terminate during the option period
Boxes left blank or vagueNot permitted, per TREC

For a seller, this means repair requests usually come through an amendment after the buyer inspects, and the option period is the time that bargaining happens.

Can I use a TREC form without an agent?

Yes. TREC's FAQ says the contract forms are available for public use, but they are intended primarily for brokers and sales agents trained in using them. It warns that a mistake in using a form may lead to financial loss or an unenforceable contract, and that a person using a form accepts all risks that come with it.

The FAQ says a license holder who fills in a form may add only factual matters and business details to a form adopted for mandatory use. If TREC has not promulgated a form that you need, TREC says to have an attorney draft it, and it notes that a license holder may not draft an instrument that transfers or affects an interest in real property.

  • A Texas real estate attorney can draft terms the forms do not cover.
  • Members of the Texas Association of Realtors can use that group's forms.
  • Your title company can answer how it handles earnest money and the option fee.

What should a seller check in the signed contract?

Before you sign a Texas contract, find the option days, the option fee, the earnest money amount and the repair choice. These are blanks or checkboxes that parties fill in, and TREC's FAQ treats complete and accurate completion as the license holder's duty.

  • The effective date is filled in.
  • The option fee amount is stated, and a due date for delivery.
  • The earnest money amount and the escrow agent are named.
  • The repair paragraph has one choice marked, not both and not neither.
  • Any addendum, such as financing or a back-up contract, is attached.

TREC says it cannot decide whether a contract with a blank effective date is valid. That question goes to a private attorney, so catch blanks before signing.

Can I end the contract, and who gets help with the paperwork?

A buyer who wants to terminate can use TREC's Notice of Buyer's Termination of Contract form, and a seller has a matching Notice of Seller's Termination form. TREC publishes both. Notices need to reach the other side in the way the contract requires, so check the notice paragraph in your form.

TREC's FAQ says license holders must use adopted contract forms and may add only factual matters and business details. It also says no TREC form is meant to be a contract for deed, and that anyone who needs something the forms do not cover should have an attorney prepare it. TREC does not decide whether a contract is valid, so a blank effective date or a disputed term goes to a private attorney.

Is an option period required in a Texas home contract?

No. TREC says the termination option is a negotiable term and a buyer does not have to pay for one. A buyer who pays the agreed fee gets the right to terminate for any reason by written notice during the option period.

How long is the option period?

The parties negotiate it, and it is written into the contract. TREC's FAQ gives no standard length, so check the number in your signed form.

What if the buyer did not pay the option fee?

Probably no unrestricted termination right. TREC's FAQ quotes the form as saying a buyer who states no fee or fails to deliver it on time loses that right under the option paragraph.

Which form applies to my Texas house sale?

Form 20-19, effective July 1, 2026, for single family homes and two to four unit residential properties. TREC lists separate forms for condos, new builds and farm and ranch property.

Can TREC decide an earnest money dispute?

No. TREC says it lacks jurisdiction over who is entitled to earnest money, and refers parties to a private attorney.

A Texas owner selling a home without an agent still has to give the buyer a Seller's Disclosure Notice, and if the house will still be encumbered by a recorded lien at closing the seller must give a separate lien disclosure at least seven days before. Those duties are in Property Code Secs. 5.008 and 5.016.

What paperwork does a Texas owner need to sell a house without an agent?

A Texas owner selling without an agent still has to hand the buyer a Seller's Disclosure Notice, use a written contract, and record a signed and acknowledged deed with the county clerk. No agent is needed for any of those steps, but each has rules attached.

The Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC) publishes the disclosure as Form 55-1, with an effective date of May 28, 2026. TREC describes it as required of sellers of previously occupied single family residences and as meant for contracts entered into on or after September 1, 2023. The notice carries the information that Section 5.008 of the Property Code calls for about material facts and the physical condition of the property.

  • Seller's Disclosure Notice (TREC 55-1) for a previously occupied single-family home
  • A federal lead-based paint disclosure if the house was built before 1978
  • A groundwater and surface water rights disclosure when the contract calls for it
  • Notice to Prospective Buyer (TREC 58-0), which covers title advice and utility district notices
  • A deed that is signed and acknowledged, then recorded in the land's home county

The TREC form page carries the current version. Sellers who are unsure which exemptions apply to their sale should ask a Texas real estate attorney, since the Property Code lists situations where the notice is not required.

Which disclosures apply, and where does each come from?

Some disclosures come from state law, some from the standard TREC contract, and one comes from federal law, so the list depends on the house and the contract.

Common disclosures for a Texas for-sale-by-owner house, with the agency that publishes each
DisclosureWhen it appliesPublished by
Seller's Disclosure Notice, Form 55-1Previously occupied single family residence, under Property Code Sec. 5.008TREC
Seller's Disclosure About Groundwater and Surface Water RightsDefault under TREC contracts unless every statement in Paragraph 7I(3) is trueTREC
Notice to Prospective Buyer, Form 58-0Abstract or title policy advice, and utility district noticesTREC
Lead-based paint disclosure and pamphletMost housing built before 1978U.S. EPA

The water disclosure is the one that surprises sellers. TREC says it is not required by any other law, so it arises only when the parties use a TREC contract, and the exemption from the Seller's Disclosure Notice does not automatically excuse it. A well, pond, lake or water tank on the lot, or any known severed or leased groundwater right, can make the form necessary.

TREC defines surface water rights as a permit, certified filing or certificate of adjudication from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality that allows diversion, impoundment or use of surface water. If you do not know whether your tract has one, ask an attorney.

What does federal law require for a house built before 1978?

The EPA's Lead-based Paint Disclosure Rule applies to most private housing built before 1978, and it puts the burden on the seller whether or not an agent is involved. The rule does not cover foreclosure sales, zero-bedroom units, housing built after 1977, or housing tested and found free of lead-based paint by a certified inspector.

  • Give the buyer the EPA pamphlet, Protect Your Family From Lead In Your Home.
  • Disclose what you know about lead-based paint and lead hazards, and hand over any records or reports.
  • Include a Lead Warning Statement in or attached to the contract, with confirmation that you complied.
  • Offer a 10-day window for a paint inspection or risk assessment, which the buyer may waive or the parties may change in writing.
  • Keep the signed disclosure for three years after the sale closes.

EPA publishes sample seller's disclosure forms in English and Spanish. A seller who fails to comply may face penalties, so an owner of an older Texas house should handle this before accepting an offer, not after.

Do I need a license to sell my own house in Texas?

TREC says a license is not required for an individual employed by a property owner to buy or sell real property on the owner's behalf, citing Rule 535.5(c). For a sale of your own house, confirm with TREC before relying on that answer.

That answer matters if title sits in an LLC or corporation and a family member or employee is handling the sale. It does not settle other situations, such as selling a property you do not own or taking a fee to market someone else's house. If the facts are unclear, a short call to a Texas real estate attorney costs less than a licensing complaint.

How do I record the deed and clear title in Texas?

A deed gets filed with the clerk of the county that holds the land, and it must be signed and acknowledged before an authorized officer such as a notary, or witnessed by two subscribing witnesses. The Texas county clerk manual lists general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's and sheriff's deeds among the instruments filed there.

Recording fees are set locally. Dallas, Denton and Ellis counties each print a $25 first-page charge on their fee schedules, and each charges $4 for later pages, with differences in add-ons. Ask the county clerk for the current fee page and any rules on return addresses, ID and payment, since those vary by county.

  • Title search. A title company or lawyer checks recorded liens, judgments and the chain of owners before closing.
  • Payoff and release. A mortgage balance is paid at closing and the lender records a release of lien.
  • Inherited houses. The State Law Library says no law forces third parties to accept an affidavit of heirship, and that a muniment of title, executor's deed or transfer on death deed may be needed instead.
  • Contracts for deed. Property Code chapter 5, subchapter D covers executory contracts for residential property, and the purchaser has a statutory right to cancel.

How do property taxes and exemptions factor into a Texas for-sale-by-owner sale?

The tax lien attaches on January 1 and the owner on that day is liable for the year, so the contract has to say who pays what for the year of sale. The Comptroller says appraisal districts value property as of January 1, tax bills go out around October 1, and unpaid taxes become delinquent on February 1 with a six percent penalty and one percent interest.

A buyer who takes title after January 1 can claim a homestead exemption for the rest of that year if the seller did not receive it. School districts must give a $140,000 residence homestead exemption, and owners 65 or older or disabled get an additional $60,000 school exemption. Sellers should bring tax receipts, exemption letters and any over-65 ceiling paperwork to the closing so the title company can prorate correctly.

Texas also sets a 10 percent annual cap on increases in appraised value for a residence homestead.

What if I am selling to stop a foreclosure?

A Texas homeowner facing non-judicial foreclosure has a short and fixed timeline, and selling before the auction is one way out. After a notice of default, the borrower may cure by paying the past-due amount within 20 days of receiving it, and the servicer must send a Notice of Sale at least 21 days before the sale.

Foreclosure auctions are public and held between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on the first Tuesday of a month, or the first Wednesday if the first Tuesday is January 1 or July 4, according to the Attorney General's informal guidance. A seller in this position should call the servicer, find out the sale date on the posted notice, and have a title company confirm the payoff before listing at a price the market will bear.

Frequently asked questions

Do I have to give a buyer a Seller's Disclosure Notice if I sell my Texas house myself?

Generally yes. TREC describes Form 55-1 as required of sellers of previously occupied single family residences, based on Property Code Sec. 5.008. Having no agent does not remove the duty, though the statute lists situations where the notice does not apply.

Is the groundwater and surface water disclosure required by Texas law?

No. TREC says it is not required by another law. It becomes part of the deal when the parties use a TREC contract, unless every statement in Paragraph 7I(3) of the One to Four Family Residential Contract is true.

What is TREC Form 58-0?

It is the Notice to Prospective Buyer. TREC says it acknowledges that the buyer was advised to have an attorney examine the abstract or to buy a title insurance policy, and it carries statutory notices that matter if the property lies in a utility district.

Does a federal lead paint disclosure apply to my Texas home?

Only if the house was built before 1978. For most private housing from that era, the EPA rule requires the pamphlet, a disclosure of what you know, a Lead Warning Statement and a 10-day inspection window for the buyer.

Where do I record the deed after a for-sale-by-owner closing in Texas?

At the office of the clerk for the county that holds the house. The deed must be signed and acknowledged before a notary or other authorized officer, or witnessed by two subscribing witnesses, and the county sets its own fee and filing rules.

Texas Property Tax Guide: Rates, Due Dates, Penalties and Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Texas

Owe Texas Property Taxes? Get a Cash Offer Before the Next Deadline

Unpaid property taxes can be paid from your sale proceeds at closing. Tell us about the house and get a written cash offer.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas has no state property tax. Local taxing units set rates, appraisal districts set values, and taxes are due by January 31 of the year after the tax year. Taxes for 2026 are due by January 31, 2027, which is a Sunday, so under Tax Code Sec. 1.06 the last day without penalty is Monday, February 1, 2027. This guide covers the vocabulary, the penalty schedule and what happens if taxes go unpaid. For county and city details, use our Texas county property tax guides.

Get My Cash Offer →

Which governments tax a Texas house, and who sends the bill?

Several local ones. The Comptroller says the state itself levies no property tax, so the county, a school district, often a city and sometimes special districts each charge a rate on the same home.

A separate appraisal district places the value. Its chief appraiser appraises each parcel as of January 1 and handles exemption requests, and a review board hears disagreements. Many units contract with the county tax assessor-collector, who mails one combined bill in October.

What does the Texas tax year look like from January to the following winter?

It runs on a fixed calendar published by the Comptroller. Ten dates matter most to a homeowner, and the table gathers them.

Property tax dates taken from the Texas Comptroller's calendar page
DateEvent
Jan. 1Value, exemption status and the year's tax lien are fixed
Apr. 1 or soon afterValue notices go out for single-family homesteads
Apr. 30Deadline for many exemption applications
May 1 or soon afterValue notices for other property
May 15Protest deadline, unless 30 days after the notice is later
July 25Chief appraiser certifies the roll
Sept. 29Most units adopt rates by this date, or within 60 days of the roll if later
Oct. 1Bills mailed
Nov. 30 and June 30Halves of a split payment
Jan. 31Final day without delinquency

Bills arrive in October and are payable on receipt, while delinquency begins the following February 1.

How does a taxing unit arrive at its rate?

By following a notice-and-hearing sequence the Comptroller calls truth-in-taxation. After the certified roll arrives, most units compute two benchmark rates before voting.

One is the no-new-revenue rate, a comparison figure that would collect the same dollars from the same properties as last year. The other is the voter-approval rate, the ceiling above which voters must approve. For most non-school units it lets operating revenue grow 3.5 percent over the prior year, plus room for debt service. Junior college and hospital districts and other special units get 8 percent. Going over the ceiling triggers an election on the next uniform election date.

  • Units post both benchmark rates on their homepages.
  • Each notice names when the vote will happen.
  • Units other than very small ones hold a public hearing.

Who has to file a rendition, and when?

Renditions concern business and other personal property more than homes. The rendition period starts January 2, and April 15 is the last day for most property types, with the chief appraiser required to extend to May 15 when asked in writing. A homeowner usually does not file one, but a landlord with equipment or a business owner with furnishings might.

When does unpaid Texas property tax turn delinquent, and what is added?

A balance still open once January ends is delinquent the next morning. That day the collector adds six percent in penalty and one percent in interest, and the Comptroller's payment page says the penalty then grows one percent monthly until it reaches twelve percent in July. Interest keeps running monthly with no ceiling.

A unit with a collection lawyer on contract may tack on up to a fifth more. Because bills must allow 21 days, a bill mailed after January 10 moves delinquency later, and the Comptroller's example has a January 15 bill going delinquent March 1.

The four-installment option for older or disabled homeowners has its first payment due by February 1, with later deadlines in the calendar on March 31, May 31 and July 31. The installment penalty is six percent of the late installment, plus one percent monthly interest.

  • A waiver of penalty and interest is possible when the owner pays within 21 days of learning about the delinquency and asks in writing before day 181.
  • Some collectors allow payment plans up to 36 months, and one is required for a residence homestead.
  • A homeowner past 65, or disabled, may pay a current bill in four installments.

Which exemptions cut the taxable value of a home?

The residence homestead exemption is the biggest one. Every school district exempts $140,000 of homestead value. Any unit may also adopt a local option cut of up to 20 percent, never below $5,000.

  • Age 65 and up, or a qualifying disability, brings an added $60,000 school exemption.
  • Disabled veterans get $5,000 to $12,000 off by rating level, and the homestead of one rated 100 percent is fully exempt.
  • A surviving spouse 55 or older can in some cases keep a late spouse's over-65 benefit.

The usual filing window closes at the end of April. A new buyer who closes after the first of the year can claim the break at once for that year when the seller had not.

What happens if a delinquent account is not paid at all?

The collection path runs from delinquent notices to an optional payment plan to a lawsuit, and court costs are added to the bill. A suit can end in an auction run by a constable or a hired agent. No statewide list exists, so look at the county clerk and tax office sites.

What a former owner can recover depends on the property type. Homestead, agricultural and mineral property carry a two-year redemption period, as a Texas Supreme Court opinion describes, and a former owner has two years to claim any excess sale proceeds. Heirs who inherit a house with delinquent years should call the tax office early, since the account may qualify for a plan.

Are there caps on how quickly a homestead bill can climb?

Yes, two of them. Per the Comptroller, a homestead's appraised value may climb at most 10 percent annually once the exemption has been in place a year, except for new improvements.

A homeowner past 65 or disabled also gets a school tax ceiling pegged to the year of qualifying. If the owner moves within Texas, a proportional share of the ceiling can go along. Counties, cities and junior college districts can adopt their own ceiling, so ask each unit whether it has done so.

What are an owner's options if the appraisal looks too high?

A protest goes to the appraisal review board, usually by May 15 or a month after the notice, whichever date falls later. After the board decides, appeals can go to district court, regular binding arbitration, or State Office of Administrative Hearings when the board's value exceeds $1,000,000.

An appeal needs at least the undisputed part of the tax paid before delinquency. Our separate protest guide covers the hearing itself.

How do unpaid taxes work when a Texas house is sold?

The yearly lien stays with the house, so title companies insist that old years be cleared. The Comptroller adds that whoever held title at the start of the year remains answerable for that year's tax and may be sued even after selling.

The title company usually pays delinquent amounts from the seller's proceeds and divides the current year between the parties. Ask the assessor-collector for a tax certificate listing every unit, and confirm what the title company will show on the settlement statement.

  • Look for delinquent years, penalties and attorney fees.
  • Ask whether a payment plan exists on the account.
  • After closing, the buyer files for the homestead exemption in the buyer's name.

Frequently asked questions

Does the state of Texas collect property tax?

No. The Comptroller says the state levies none, and local taxing units set rates and collect the money.

When must Texas property tax be paid?

Bills are mailed in October with payment due on arrival. Delinquency starts February 1 for anything open after January 31. Split payment, where allowed, means halves due November 30 and June 30.

What is the late charge on Texas property tax?

Six percent penalty and one percent interest land on day one of delinquency. The penalty then climbs one percent a month to twelve percent in July.

What size is the Texas homestead exemption?

School districts must exempt $140,000, with $60,000 extra for older or disabled owners. Other units may add local exemptions.

Can delinquent tax be paid out of a sale?

Yes. Title companies usually settle it from the seller's proceeds, since the lien stays with the house.

Texas Homestead Exemption: Amounts, Over-65 Rules and Appraisal Cap

Cash Home Buyers in Texas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Texas Homestead Exemption: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Texas Homestead Exemption sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

The Texas residence homestead exemption takes $140,000 off the value of your home for school district taxes, and homeowners who are 65 or older or disabled get an additional $60,000. The amounts are in Tax Code Sec. 11.13(b) and (c) and Texas Constitution Article VIII Sec. 1-b. You apply through your county appraisal district.

Ready to sell your Texas home?
We buy as-is, pay off taxes from the proceeds and charge no commission.
Get My Cash Offer →

What does the Texas homestead exemption do for a homeowner?

It removes part of your home's appraised value from the base that local taxing units tax, so the bill shrinks even though the market value does not change. Appraisal districts set value as of January 1, so your status on that date drives the year's bill. The Texas Comptroller lays out three layers: a mandatory school district exemption, optional local exemptions, and extra relief for older or disabled owners.

Texas has no state property tax. Each taxing unit applies the exemption to its own levy, so two neighbors served by different units can see different savings.

How much is the general residence homestead exemption?

Tax Code Sec. 11.13(b) sets a $140,000 school district exemption on a residence homestead. Under Sec. 11.13(n) any other unit may choose a percentage exemption, capped at 20 percent of value, with a $5,000 minimum.

  • School districts: $140,000, mandatory.
  • Cities, counties and others: optional, at the unit's discretion.
  • Counties with farm-to-market or flood control levies: $3,000 (Sec. 11.13(a)).

Ask your appraisal district which units serving your address have adopted a local option, because the Comptroller describes it as a choice each unit makes.

Who qualifies as the owner of a homestead?

Two tests apply: you own an interest in the house, and it is where you mainly live. A second claimed homestead, in Texas or elsewhere, disqualifies you.

A mid-year purchase still earns the exemption for the remaining months if the seller was not already getting it. Heirs absent from the recorded deed show the appraisal district an ownership affidavit, the prior owner's death certificate, a utility bill and any court record citation.
