What extra relief exists at age 65 or with a disability?

Age 65 or disability adds $60,000 at the school district level (Sec. 11.13(c)). Local units may match with their own under Sec. 11.13(d), starting at $3,000.

Disability is judged by the Social Security benefit definition. In some cases a widow or widower aged 55 or more keeps the late spouse's over-65 benefit.

These owners also receive a freeze on school tax. Sec. 11.26 bars the district from raising their total yearly bill on the homestead, using the tax of the first year they qualified as the base. The freeze can follow the owner to a new Texas homestead, in proportion, and can continue for a surviving spouse aged 55 or older. Added improvements beyond ordinary repairs can lift it. Sec. 11.261 allows counties, cities and junior college districts to adopt their own.

How does the 10 percent appraisal cap work?

Once you qualify, appraised value on the homestead may climb at most 10 percent a year, new improvements aside. Sec. 23.23 takes the lesser of market value or last year's appraised value plus 10 percent plus improvements.

It starts the January 1 after your first qualifying year. A higher rate from a taxing unit can still raise the bill, since the cap governs value only.

What do disabled veterans receive?

Disabled veterans get an exemption on any one property they own, scaled to their VA disability rating. The Comptroller prints these amounts under Sec. 11.22.

Sec. 11.22 disabled veteran exemption, as printed by the Texas Comptroller
VA disability ratingExemption up to
10% to 29%$5,000
30% to 49%$7,500
50% to 69%$10,000
70% to 100%$12,000

A veteran aged 65 or older with a rating of at least 10 percent, a veteran who is totally blind in one or both eyes, or one who lost use of a limb may receive $12,000. An unmarried surviving spouse and children under 18 may qualify too.

At a 100 percent rating, or 100 percent unemployability, the whole residence homestead is exempt under Sec. 11.131, and an unmarried surviving spouse may keep it on stated conditions. A charity-donated homestead falls under Sec. 11.132, where the exempt share follows the rating. Sec. 11.133 fully exempts the home of a surviving spouse of a service member killed in the line of duty.

How do the layers combine for different owners?

Think of the exemption as a stack that grows with your circumstances. Each layer applies only to the taxing units that grant it.

  • Any residence homestead owner: the mandatory $140,000 school district exemption.
  • Owner aged 65 or older, or disabled: that same $140,000 plus $60,000, along with the school tax freeze.
  • Disabled veteran: a separate exemption on one property, scaled from $5,000 to $12,000 by rating, or total at a 100 percent rating on the residence homestead.
  • Any owner in a unit with a local option: a percentage exemption of up to 20 percent of value on top.

The Comptroller's pages describe each as a distinct provision, so an owner who fits two groups should ask the appraisal district how the two apply together on the actual bill.

What should an applicant bring to the appraisal district?

Bring proof of ownership and proof that the house is your main home, such as a utility bill. Each district decides what it accepts, so call the office before you go, and file before the spring cutoff so the exemption reaches the bill mailed that fall.

  • The deed, or for an heir the ownership affidavit and death certificate.
  • A current utility bill showing the property address.
  • For age, disability or a VA rating, whatever proof the district accepts; ask which documents it wants before you file.
  • The form that matches your exemption: 50-114 for homestead, 50-135 for the disabled veteran exemption.

Applying for a veteran exemption does not require waiting for the next spring cycle in every case, because Sec. 11.22 allows late applications for up to five years after the delinquency date.

When and where do you apply?

The county appraisal district takes the application; the school district and Comptroller do not. For the general homestead exemption the filing must come before May 1, and April 30 also closes some other exemption and special-appraisal applications.

  • Homestead exemptions use Form 50-114.
  • The disabled veteran exemption under Sec. 11.22 uses Form 50-135.
  • Veterans under Sec. 11.22 get up to five years past the delinquency date to apply, and the surviving spouse of a veteran with a donated homestead gets two.

Value notices for single-family homesteads start around April 1. Disputing the number is a separate step from the exemption and has its own cutoff, usually May 15 unless 30 days after delivery falls later.

How does the exemption matter when you sell?

Your exemption leaves with your ownership, but that year's lien stays on the land. It attaches January 1 for taxes, penalties and interest, so unpaid amounts normally get cleared at closing.

Whoever owned on January 1 is liable for the year's bill and can be sued after selling. Delinquency starts February 1 for bills mailed in October, with penalty and interest added.

For a sale involving back taxes, unrecorded heirs or a house you have moved out of, get a payoff from the tax office and your exemption status from the district first.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Texas homestead exemption automatic?

No, you must apply with Form 50-114 at the appraisal district, in general before May 1.

Can I get both the $140,000 and the $60,000 school exemptions?

Yes, for owners aged 65 or older or disabled, the two stack: $140,000 under Sec. 11.13(b) plus $60,000 under Sec. 11.13(c).

Does the 10 percent cap lower my tax rate?

No. It slows growth in appraised value only. Each unit sets its rate separately, and new improvements come on top of the capped value.

Can a surviving spouse keep the over-65 exemption?

In some cases, if the spouse is 55 or older; the school tax ceiling may continue too. The appraisal district can confirm your situation.

What if I inherited a house and am not on the deed?

Bring four items to the district: an ownership affidavit, the death certificate, a recent utility bill and any court record citation.

Cash Home Buyers in Texas

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Texas Property Tax Protest sale

Last updated November 14, 2026.

To protest your Texas appraisal, file written notice with the appraisal review board by May 15 or 30 days after the notice was delivered to you, whichever is later. That rule is in Tax Code Sec. 41.44(a)(1). This guide follows the Comptroller's protest page and Tax Code Chapters 41 and 42 through the ARB hearing and appeals.

Tired of the tax bills?
We buy as-is, pay taxes from the proceeds and charge no commission.

What is the deadline to protest a Texas property appraisal?

In most cases it is May 15 or 30 days after the appraisal district's notice, whichever is later. The Comptroller's protest page gives this rule and notes in one place that the 30 days run from the date the district mails the notice.

The district must send a notice of appraised value by May 1, or April 1 for a residence homestead, or soon after, when the value is higher than last year. That notice explains how to file and mentions the informal conference option. Read it the day it arrives and note the mailing date.

How do you file a Texas protest?

File Form 50-132, Property Owner's Notice of Protest, with the appraisal review board (ARB). The Comptroller also says the form is optional, because a written notice that names the property, the owner and some dissatisfaction with a district decision is enough.

  • Use Form 50-162 if you want an agent to represent you at the hearing.
  • Lessees who must reimburse the owner's taxes may protest if the owner does not.
  • Off-shore workers and full-time military members may be entitled to file late.

Keep a copy and proof of the filing date, since the deadline controls whether you get a hearing.

What can a Texas owner protest?

You can protest the appraised value or any district action about your property. The Comptroller lists value, exemptions, special appraisal qualification and the circuit breaker limitation as hearing subjects.

Many owners ask whether the tax bill itself can be protested. It cannot, because the ARB does not set rates. The Comptroller says neither the ARB nor the appraisal district sets your taxes, and the ARB cannot consider your personal finances. Its job is to certify value based on what the market dictates.

How does the protest fit into the rest of the Texas tax calendar?

The protest season sits between the spring notices and the summer roll. The Comptroller's calendar has the ARB beginning to hear protests around May 15, approving the appraisal records by July 20 and the chief appraiser certifying the roll to each taxing unit by July 25. The ARB may hold off approval if more than 5 percent of total appraised value is still under protest.

Taxing units then adopt rates by about the end of September, and bills follow on October 1. A successful protest changes the value that those rates are applied to. It does not change the rate.

  • Spring: value notice arrives and the protest window opens.
  • Late spring and summer: informal conferences and ARB hearings.
  • July: records approved and roll certified.
  • October: bills mailed, with the tax due by the following January 31.

What happens between filing and the ARB hearing?

You may ask for an informal conference with the appraisal district, and many protests end there. If not, the case goes to a formal hearing.

The ARB must send notice of the hearing date, time, place and subject at least 15 days in advance. At least 14 days before, the district must send the Comptroller's Taxpayer Assistance Pamphlet, the adopted ARB procedures and a statement that you can request copies of the evidence the district will use. You can attend in person, by phone or videoconference, or file a written affidavit. Counties above 120,000 people deliver electronic notices and reminders when you give an email address or number.

What evidence helps at a Texas ARB hearing?

Bring proof of value, since saying the district is wrong is not enough. The Comptroller names the types of material that help.

  • Photographs of your property and comparable ones.
  • Repair receipts or estimates.
  • Sales price records, such as listings or closing statements.
  • Median level of appraisal calculations, for an equal and uniform protest.
  • Affidavits, engineering reports, surveys and deed records.

You choose whether to present before or after the district representative. Both sides may present evidence, question witnesses and state an opinion of value. Stay on the facts about value. The ARB's decision binds only for the tax year in question.

What if you miss the protest deadline?

A late protest can still get a hearing if you show good cause before the ARB approves the appraisal records. The Comptroller warns that missing good cause, or filing after approval, can end the right to protest.

Other late routes exist for narrower problems, and each requires you to avoid letting the tax go delinquent.

  • Failure to receive a notice the district was required to send.
  • A motion for correction when a residence homestead was valued at least one-fourth too high.
  • A motion for correction when other property was valued at least one-third too high.
  • A clerical error, duplicate appraisal or ownership error, which can reach back through the current year and five earlier years.
  • A joint motion with the chief appraiser, which the ARB approves if both agree.

What is limited binding arbitration, and how is it different from an appeal?

It is a narrow tool for process problems. After filing a protest, an owner who believes the ARB or the chief appraiser skipped a procedural requirement can ask the Comptroller's office for limited binding arbitration to compel compliance. It does not reopen the value itself.

The Comptroller runs a separate web page for the process. Owners who simply disagree with the value should stay with the hearing and the appeal routes in the table below.

Who can speak for you at the hearing?

Owners and lessees may name someone to represent them. The Comptroller's page points to Form 50-162, Appointment of Agent for Property Tax Matters, for that purpose. An agent can attend, present evidence and question the district's witness on your behalf.

The hearing is not a place to argue about the size of your bill or your income. The Comptroller says the ARB may weigh general economic and environmental influences on value but not an owner's personal finances. The Comptroller's office also cannot advise on or step into a matter under protest, so questions about a live case go to the appraisal district or the ARB.

After the hearing, the ARB sends a written order by email or certified mail. Keep it, because every appeal deadline runs from receiving it.

Where can you appeal after the ARB rules?

You have three main paths, set out in the table from the Comptroller's protest page. The ARB's written order arrives by email or certified mail.

Appeal options after an ARB order, from the Comptroller's protest page
OptionDeadline from the orderNotes
State district courtPetition within 60 days of receiving the orderCounty where the property sits; consult an attorney first
Regular binding arbitrationRequest to the Comptroller within 60 days of noticeHomestead at any value, or property of $5 million or less; deposit required
State Office of Administrative HearingsNotice to chief appraiser within 30 days; $1,500 deposit within 90 daysARB value over $1 million; value or unequal appraisal only; not industrial property

In every case, pay at least the undisputed tax before the delinquency date. A court may excuse prepayment after a hearing if you file an oath of inability to pay.

Does a protest matter if you plan to sell the house?

It can, because the appraised value drives the bill that is prorated at closing and a lower value for the year lowers the amount owed. If the ARB rules in your favor, the chief appraiser notifies the taxing units, and the units send any refund when taxes were already paid.

Special ARB panels hear commercial, utility, industrial and multifamily property valued at or above a threshold. The Comptroller lists $62,883,169 for 2026. Single-family owners will not reach that level.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Texas protest deadline?

May 15 or 30 days after the appraisal district's notice, whichever is later. The Comptroller says the 30 days run from the mailing date.

Do I need a lawyer to protest in Texas?

No. You can file a simple written notice and appear yourself, and Form 50-162 lets you name an agent if you prefer. The Comptroller advises talking to an attorney before a district court petition.

Can I protest my tax rate?

No. The ARB hears value and related district actions, and it does not set rates. Taxing units adopt rates after notice and hearing.

What if I miss the protest date?

Ask the ARB for a late hearing and show good cause, before it approves the appraisal records. Some narrower correction motions also exist, as long as taxes are not delinquent.

How long do I have to appeal an ARB order?

Within 60 days of receiving the order for district court or regular binding arbitration, and within 30 days for the SOAH notice if the ARB value is over $1 million.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

After a Texas tax sale, a former owner of a homestead can redeem the property on or before the second anniversary of the purchaser's deed filing, but must pay a premium of 25 percent in the first year and 50 percent in the second. Other property has only 180 days, and the premium cannot exceed 25 percent. These rules come from Tax Code Chapter 34.

How does a Texas property go to a tax sale?

Each year's taxes are secured by a lien that arises on the first day of January, and a bill left unpaid can end in a suit and then an auction of the property. The sale is a tax foreclosure auction, and the winning bidder receives a deed afterward.

The ladder runs in order: delinquency notices, an optional installment plan, then a suit by the taxing unit, with court costs added to the bill. Once a bill goes delinquent the Comptroller says the cost climbs: an initial penalty and interest charge is added, the penalty grows each month until July, and interest has no ceiling. Collection attorneys hired by the unit can add a further charge.

Who runs the sale and where is it held?

Tax foreclosure sales are auctions, typically run by the constable or an agent the taxing unit hires.

The State Law Library tells buyers and owners to check the county clerk or county tax office websites for sale notices. Because each taxing unit and county handles notices its own way, call the tax office that bills the property instead of trusting a general list. The lien survives a change of ownership, so a buyer at an ordinary sale who skips the tax check can end up with the liability.

Can the former owner get the property back after a Texas tax sale?

Yes, in a limited window, and the cost depends on the kind of property. Tax Code Section 34.21 governs redemption, as a Texas Supreme Court opinion explains.

Redemption rules for land auctioned for taxes, as described by the Texas Supreme Court
Kind of propertyRedemption periodPremium
Homestead, agricultural or mineral interestTwo years after the buyer's deed is filed25 percent in the first year, 50 percent in the second
Other property180th day after the deed is filedNot over 25 percent

Source: Texas Supreme Court opinion on Tax Code Section 34.21.

On top of that the owner repays the winning bid, the deed recording fee and the back charges. The purchaser must itemize those costs within 10 days of a written request, so a redeeming owner should put the request on paper.

Who gets the money when a property sells for more than the taxes owed?

Money left over once the tax debt and costs are paid is called excess proceeds, and the former owner has two years from the sale to claim them. Sections 34.03 and 34.04 of the Tax Code govern the process, according to the State Law Library.

If you suspect money is waiting for you, contact the court that ordered the sale and the tax office. Keep proof of your ownership and your current mailing address with your claim. Heirs of a deceased owner should be ready to show how they inherited, since the claim follows the same ownership questions that arise in probate.

What should a buyer check before bidding at a tax sale?

A buyer should confirm what the deed will and will not do, because the redemption right can reopen the deal after the sale.

  • Find out from the tax office which units' taxes the sale covers.
  • Check whether the property is a homestead, farmland or has a mineral interest, since these have the longer redemption period.
  • Review the county records for other liens. The comptroller files state tax liens with the county clerk, who records them in the state tax lien book.
  • Plan for the possibility of an occupant. If someone is living there, expect to need a court case to get possession.

The county clerk is the county recorder, so the clerk's office is also where the deed will be recorded afterward.

How can an owner avoid a tax sale in Texas?

Pay before the delinquency date or work out a payment plan. Plans on delinquent bills can run as long as 36 months with some collectors, and a homestead owner is entitled to one.

Penalty and interest waivers exist for many cases, but they require quick payment and a written request, so ask the collector for the exact deadlines on your bill. Older or disabled homeowners can split delinquent tax into four installments, and veterans with a disability rating may qualify for an exemption. If you are behind and thinking of selling, a sale that pays the tax at closing ends the lien problem before a lawsuit begins.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Does a tax sale affect a seller trying to sell a house?

It does, because a buyer cannot get clear title until the delinquent taxes are paid. A seller with unpaid tax should get a payoff number from the title company and pay the tax from closing funds.

The January 1 owner owes that year's tax, and a suit can still reach that person after a sale. Get the paid-in-full records from the tax office after closing and keep them.

What does the Texas property tax calendar mean for a seller?

Values are fixed on January 1, bills are mailed near October 1, and a split payment lets an owner pay half in November and the balance in June.

Most owners need to pay by January 31, because taxes unpaid on February 1 are delinquent. Late-mailed bills get a later delinquency date. An owner who disagrees with the appraised value takes that dispute to the appraisal review board, generally by mid-May. After the board, an owner can appeal to district court, binding arbitration, or the state's administrative hearings office when the board value tops $1,000,000.

  • Section 23.23 caps yearly increases in a homestead's appraised value at 10 percent.
  • Section 11.26 can freeze school tax for an older or disabled homeowner.
  • An owner who appeals should still pay the amount not in dispute on time.

What help exists for owners who are behind on taxes?

Ask the county tax assessor-collector about installment plans, waivers and exemptions before a suit is filed. Many taxing units contract with the assessor-collector, so one office often handles the bill for several units.

The Comptroller notes that those homeowners can pay delinquent amounts in installments, with a 6 percent charge on the late installment and monthly interest. Disabled veterans should ask the appraisal district about the exemption that matches their VA rating.

What should an owner do after receiving a notice of tax suit or sale?

Act on it the same week. Call the tax office named on the notice, ask for the full payoff with court costs included, and ask whether the collector offers a payment plan for the delinquent years. Collection ladders in Texas move from notices to a plan to a lawsuit, and each step adds expense, so the cheapest moment to resolve a debt is the earliest one.

  • Write down the cause number and the court named on any suit papers.
  • Ask the clerk of that court how an excess proceeds claim would be filed.
  • Keep copies of every payment receipt, since the owner of record remains answerable for the year's tax.
  • If you plan to sell, give the title company the tax office's payoff letter right away.

Heirs and family members sometimes learn about a delinquent bill only after the owner has died. In that situation the first job is to sort out who holds title, because the person who can negotiate with the tax office is the owner or someone authorized to act for the estate.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a redemption period after a Texas tax sale?

Yes. Homestead, farm and mineral property carries a two-year window. Other property gets roughly half a year.

What premium does a redeeming owner pay?

For the two-year category, the premium is 25 percent if the owner redeems in year one and 50 percent in year two. Other property carries a premium of no more than 25 percent.

When does the right to claim leftover sale money end?

Two years after the sale. Claims go through the court that ordered the sale under Tax Code Sections 34.03 and 34.04.

When do Texas property taxes become delinquent?

Usually on February 1 following the bill year, when penalty and interest start to run.

Where do I find tax sale listings?

No single statewide list exists. Check the county clerk and county tax office websites, or call the tax office that bills the property.

Texas Real Estate Agent Commission: What the Law Says and Your Options

Cash Home Buyers in Texas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Texas Real Estate Agent Commission sale

Skip the Agent Commission: Get a Cash Offer for Your Texas House

Our cash offers carry no agent commission and no fees. Tell us about the property.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas law does not set real estate commission rates. The Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC) says on its consumer page that it does not regulate fees paid to any license holder, and that all fees are set by your agreement with each professional. The TREC resale contract says the same about brokerage compensation.

Want to avoid the commission?
Our cash offers carry zero commission, zero fees and zero closing costs, and we buy as-is.

Does Texas law set a real estate agent commission rate?

No. The Texas Real Estate Commission says it does not regulate the fees paid to any license holder, including buyer's agents, seller's agents, brokers, inspectors and appraisers, and that all fees come from your agreement with each professional. Anyone quoting a statewide percentage as a legal rate is describing a habit, not a rule.

TREC's consumer guide adds one instruction: read the fees in any representation or service agreement before you sign it.

What changed for buyer agreements and compensation in 2026?

Legislation from the 89th Texas Legislative Session changed the Real Estate License Act so that a license holder working with a residential buyer needs a written agreement before showing a home. If no home will be shown, the agreement is needed before the agent presents an offer for the buyer. TREC's article says the changes apply as of January 1, 2026.

The agreement has to state the amount or rate of the broker's compensation and how it will be figured. It also has to say in conspicuous language that broker compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable. Commercial buyers and tenants fall outside the written-agreement rule.

  • Services the license holder will provide.
  • An end date for the agreement.
  • Whether it is exclusive or non-exclusive.
  • Whether the license holder represents the buyer.
  • The compensation amount or rate and how it is determined.

How long can a showing-only agreement last?

A non-representation, showing-only agreement can run no more than 14 days and must be non-exclusive, per TREC's article. A full representation agreement can narrow the services an agent offers, such as limiting them to showings, but cannot waive the minimum duties owed to a client.

For a Texas seller, the effect shows up in the offers you receive. A buyer's agent now arrives with a signed agreement that spells out how that agent expects to be paid, so the question of who covers that fee comes up early in negotiation instead of late.

What do agents owe me, and who handles complaints?

TREC's consumer guide says brokers and sales agents must put the client's interests above all others, acting as fiduciaries. The minimum services are telling the client any material information about the property or transaction, answering questions and presenting offers and counteroffers, and treating all parties honestly and fairly.

Agents must hand you the Information About Brokerage Services form the first time you discuss a specific property, along with the Consumer Protection Notice. If you think an agent is not treating you fairly, TREC accepts complaints and can act against a license holder who breaks the rules. TREC's license holder lookup shows whether a person holds an active license and any discipline.

Can an agent rebate part of the commission?

Yes. TREC's FAQ says a license holder may rebate part of the compensation to a party in the transaction without violating the license act or rules. If the rebate goes to a party the agent does not represent, the agent must first get the consent of the party the agent does represent, under Rule 535.147(d).

The same FAQ says an agent who advertises a rebate must follow Rule 535.155, and that a rebate may be limited by the buyer's lender. A listing broker also may not share compensation with someone who acts as a broker without a broker license, and the FAQ gives an attorney acting as buyer's agent as an example.

Do open houses and showings change who an agent works for?

They can. TREC's article on the 2026 changes says an agent hosting an open house who belongs to the listing broker's office only has to disclose that the agent represents the owner. A showing agent from another brokerage must hand over the Information About Brokerage Services form and sign a written agreement with a visiting buyer before the buyer starts viewing the home.

The article says a buyer who refuses to sign cannot be shown the property, and that license holders can face discipline for skipping the written agreement. For you as a Texas seller, that means a stranger at your open house may be asked to sign paperwork at the door, which is a legal requirement for the agent and not a sign of anything wrong with your listing.

The same article says two references to subagency were removed from the License Act. Subagency has not disappeared as a legal idea, so ask your broker or an attorney if a situation seems to involve it.

How does TREC treat commission sharing and trust accounts?

A listing broker may not share compensation with someone who acts as a broker without holding a broker license. TREC's FAQ applies this to an attorney who represents a buyer: the listing broker must still present the attorney's offer to the seller and tell the seller about the prohibition, and the seller and buyer may work out payment to a Texas attorney between themselves.

The same FAQ says a listing broker may agree to reduce the commission at a seller's request without breaking the splitting prohibition. Brokers who hold earnest money or other funds in a trust account must provide a monthly accounting when there has been activity, and must keep trust and escrow records for four years from the date the record is received or created.

  • Ask the broker where earnest money will be held.
  • Ask how a commission reduction would be written into the listing agreement.
  • Ask whether any buyer's attorney is involved, and how that attorney is paid.

What should I compare before I sign a listing agreement?

Put each offer on the same footing by comparing what reaches you after every cost. Commission is one line. Repairs, seller concessions, closing costs and any compensation you agree to pay toward the buyer's agent are others, and each is a contract term you can negotiate.

Terms TREC says belong in your agreement or contract
TermWhere TREC says it lives
Listing broker feeYour agreement with the broker, not set by TREC
Buyer agent compensationWritten buyer agreement, stated as amount or rate
Rebates to a partyRule 535.147(d) consent rule
Representation and dutiesInformation About Brokerage Services form

Ask your agent which of these appear in the paperwork you are asked to sign, and get each in writing.

What if I would rather sell without an agent commission?

You can list with a broker, sell yourself, or sell to a buyer who purchases directly, and each carries different costs and duties. A sale without a listing broker has no listing commission, but it also has no agent handling showings, paperwork or negotiation. TREC's contract forms are written for license holders, and TREC says complex or specialized situations may call for an attorney.

If the sale involves a buyer's agent, that agent's written agreement with the buyer states how the agent expects to be paid, and you can ask to see how it applies to your sale before you accept an offer.

Frequently asked questions

Is real estate commission set by law in Texas?

No. TREC says it does not regulate fees paid to any license holder, and all fees are set by your agreement with each professional.

Must a Texas buyer sign something with an agent before touring a home?

Yes, for residential buyers. TREC says a written agreement is required before showing a home or, if none is shown, before presenting an offer.

Does the written buyer agreement say how the agent gets paid?

Yes. It must state the compensation amount or rate, how it is determined, and conspicuous wording that compensation is not set by law and is negotiable.

Can an agent give back part of a commission?

Yes. TREC's FAQ says a rebate to a party is permitted, and consent of the agent's own client is required first when the rebate goes to a party the agent does not represent.

Where do I complain about an agent?

File a complaint with TREC, which can act against a license holder who breaks the rules. Disputes over who gets earnest money are outside what TREC decides.

Texas Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale: State and Federal Rules

Cash Home Buyers in Texas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Texas Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale sale
  • Turn the Texas Capital Gains Tax on a Home Sale offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling Your Texas Home? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is and close on your timeline. Tell us about the house.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Texas has no state income tax, and the federal home sale exclusion lets many sellers exclude the first $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 for a married couple filing jointly. The Texas Comptroller states that Texas has no state income tax, and IRS Publication 523 sets the exclusion and its tests. This guide summarizes those tests.

Ready to sell?
We buy as-is with no commission, and you choose the closing date.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Texas tax profit from selling a house?

Texas does not tax it. The Comptroller's office states that Texas has no state income tax, so a home sale adds nothing to a state return because there is no state return to file.

The federal government is the only income tax collector in a Texas home sale. Texas homeowners still deal with property taxes at closing, covered below, but those are charges for owning the house and not a tax on profit.

How big is the federal exclusion for a Texas home sale?

The IRS caps the tax-free gain at $250,000 for one filer and $500,000 for spouses filing together, as Topic 701 explains. The cap applies to profit only. Profit is what remains after subtracting adjusted basis from the amount realized, a definition Topic 409 gives.

Basis starts with the cost of the house, including sales tax and purchase expenses. Topic 703 says improvements that add value raise it, while items like insurance reimbursements for casualty losses reduce it. A Texas owner who finished a garage apartment or replaced a roof should dig out those receipts. A long-held house with no upgrades tends to carry a low basis and therefore a larger gain.

Losses get no relief. Topic 409 states that a loss on personal-use property, a home included, is not deductible.

Which two tests decide eligibility?

Ownership and use. Each is measured over the five-year window that ends on the closing date, and Topic 701 summarizes them below.

Federal home-sale exclusion tests as summarized by the IRS
ItemIRS description
OwnershipTwo years of ownership inside the window
UseTwo years living there as a main residence inside the window
OverlapThe two years of ownership and use can come from different periods
Spouses filing jointlyOne spouse can satisfy ownership; each spouse must satisfy use
Back-to-back salesGenerally blocked if another home's gain was excluded within the prior two years
Extended official dutyWindow can be suspended up to a decade for service members, Foreign Service and intelligence personnel

Source: IRS Topic 701. Publication 523 lists partial-exclusion situations and exceptions.

How do I estimate my own gain before listing?

Work through the pieces in order and keep paper copies of each. The IRS describes the building blocks across Topics 409, 701 and 703.

  • Start with what you paid for the house, plus purchase-related costs such as sales tax that Topic 703 counts as part of basis.
  • Add the cost of improvements that added value, and subtract items that reduce basis, such as insurance reimbursements for casualty losses.
  • Take the amount you expect to realize from the sale and subtract adjusted basis to get the gain.
  • Compare that gain with the $250,000 or $500,000 ceiling if you pass both tests.
  • Only the part above the ceiling, if any, goes into the capital gain rate bands.

Sellers in Texas often forget that a home bought decades ago with little paper trail can still have a documented basis through closing statements and permit records. County clerk deed records and your original settlement statement are a good place to start.

What federal rates hit gain above the exclusion?

A long-term gain on a Texas house is taxed at 0, 15 or 20 percent depending on taxable income, with the IRS printing its 2025 thresholds on Topic 409.

  • The 0 percent band ends at $48,350 of taxable income for single and separate filers, $96,700 for joint filers, and $64,750 for heads of household.
  • The 15 percent band runs above those levels to $533,400 single, $300,000 separate, $600,050 joint, and $566,700 head of household.
  • Income past the 15 percent ceiling is taxed at 20 percent on the excess.

Depreciation claimed while the house was a rental can be taxed at up to 25 percent as unrecaptured section 1250 gain, according to that same page. Short-term results are taxed like wages. Thresholds change by year, so look up the IRS figures that match the year your sale closes.

What changes if the house was inherited or rented out?

The simple exclusion story shifts in both cases. For an inherited house, the IRS routes basis questions to Publication 551, since basis is not simply what the heir paid. Topic 409 also flags special holding-period rules for property acquired from a decedent and refers readers to Publication 544.

For a house that spent years as a rental, depreciation reduces basis, and Publication 523 handles homes with rental or business use. Title questions for heirs are covered on this site's Texas affidavit of heirship and probate pages.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When does a Texas seller have to report the sale?

Whenever a Form 1099-S arrives, even if every dollar of gain is excludable, and whenever some gain cannot be excluded. The IRS directs filers to Form 8949 and Schedule D for the actual reporting.

A seller who carried the financing over later years may spread the gain using the installment method. Topic 701 says the home-sale exclusion stays available in that case. Large taxable gains can also trigger estimated payments, and Publication 505 covers that rule.

How does the one-year holding rule differ from the exclusion tests?

It is a separate clock. Under Topic 409, an asset kept for more than a year yields a long-term result, and one kept a year or less yields a short-term result taxed at ordinary rates. Counting begins the day after acquisition and includes the sale day.

Picture two sellers. One lived in a house for 18 months and then sold: the holding period is long-term, yet the two-year exclusion tests are unmet. Another owned for 25 months but rented the place out for most of that time: ownership is satisfied while use may not be. Mark both dates on a calendar well ahead of any contract.

Gifts and inherited property get special treatment, and Publication 544 covers them.

Which Texas charges still show up at closing?

Property tax. The Comptroller explains that local units, not the state, levy it, and that appraisal districts value each parcel annually as of January 1. Because that is the date the year's lien attaches, a buyer's title company will want it settled.

Request the tax certificate early and compare it to what the county tax assessor-collector shows. The Comptroller's payment page lists the penalty and interest schedule that applies to unpaid bills.

Closing also brings a federal filing detail worth knowing early. If you receive a Form 1099-S, the IRS has a record of the sale whether or not you owe anything. Matching your return to that form avoids notices later, and a tax preparer can check the entries against your settlement statement.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Texas capital gains tax on real estate?

No. The Comptroller states that Texas has no state income tax, so a home sale produces no state capital gains return. The federal rules in IRS Topic 701 and Topic 409 still apply.

How long must I live in a Texas home to avoid federal tax on the gain?

At least two years of both ownership and use inside the five years before closing. The months need not be consecutive, and the two periods may be different stretches.

What is the exclusion for a married couple selling a Texas house?

$500,000 of gain on a joint return. One spouse can meet the ownership test, but each spouse must meet the use test on their own, per IRS Topic 701.

Can I deduct a loss when I sell my Texas home for less than I paid?

No. IRS Topic 409 says losses from the sale of personal-use property, including your home, are not tax deductible.

Where do I report a Texas home sale?

On Form 8949 and Schedule D when reporting is required, which includes any sale that generated a Form 1099-S. Publication 523 has the worksheets. A tax professional can confirm what fits your facts.

Texas 1031 Exchange: What the IRS Says About Like-Kind Real Estate

Cash Home Buyers in Texas
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Selling a Texas Investment Property? Get a Cash Offer

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Under Section 1031, an exchange of real property held for business or investment solely for other business or investment real property of like kind generally defers recognition of gain or loss. Texas has no state income tax, so the issue is federal. This guide uses the IRS real estate tax tips page and Publication 523.

Selling a rental?
We buy rental and investment houses as-is, occupied or vacant, with no commission.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is a Section 1031 exchange for Texas real estate?

It is a tax rule that lets an owner of business or investment real property swap it for other business or investment real property and generally skip recognizing the gain or loss at that time. The IRS says you must recognize gain only to the extent you also receive cash or other non-like-kind property, and you cannot recognize a loss. Texas owners use the same federal rule as everyone else.

Since January 1, 2018, the rule covers real property only. Exchanges of equipment, vehicles, artwork, collectibles and patents no longer qualify, apart from certain mutual ditch, reservoir and irrigation stock. A Texas rental house, apartment building, office or tract of land can qualify. Real property held primarily for sale does not.

This page explains what the IRS publishes. A tax adviser or a qualified intermediary should confirm how it applies to your sale.

Which properties count as like-kind?

Real properties are generally like-kind to each other, whether improved or unimproved. The IRS gives the example that an apartment building would generally be like-kind to another apartment building, and it says properties are like-kind when they share the same nature or character, even if grade or quality differs.

One limit applies to every investor: real property in the United States is not like-kind to real property outside the United States. So a Texas duplex can be swapped for land in another state, but not for a property abroad.

  • Qualifies: a Texas rental house exchanged for a fourplex held as an investment.
  • Qualifies: unimproved land exchanged for improved commercial property, if both are held for business or investment.
  • Does not qualify: a house you hold mainly to resell, or a house you use solely as your personal residence.

How do the 45-day and 180-day deadlines work?

A deferred exchange has two clocks that start when you transfer the property you give up. The IRS instructions say replacement property must be identified within 45 days, and received by the earlier of 180 days or the due date of your tax return, including extensions, for the year of the transfer.

Timing rules from the IRS Form 8824 instructions
StepDeadlineWhat the IRS says
Identify replacement propertyWithin 45 days of the transferSigned written document, clear description, sent to the right person
Receive replacement propertyEarlier of day 180 or the return due dateCounts the due date with extensions
Report the exchangeWith the return for the transfer yearFile Form 8824

For real property, the written identification must describe it by legal description, street address or a distinguishable name. If you receive the replacement property before day 45 ends, you are treated as meeting the identification rule. Because the 180-day period can be cut short by the return due date, an exchange that closes late in the year may need an extension of the tax return to use the full 180 days.

What role does a qualified intermediary play?

In a deferred exchange, the IRS says that using a qualified intermediary (QI) lets the transfer of the property given up and the receipt of replacement property be treated as a like-kind exchange.

Related parties and your agents cannot serve as the QI. The IRS calls them disqualified persons, and the instructions point to Publication 544 for details. If the QI causes you to miss a timing rule, the transaction does not qualify as a deferred exchange, and the gain may be taxable in the year you transferred the property. The instructions describe a narrow exception when a QI defaults because of bankruptcy or receivership.

Pick the intermediary before the sale closes. The Texas side of that process is the same as any sale: a title company, a deed recorded with the county clerk where the property sits, and clear records.

Can I use a 1031 exchange on my Texas home?

Not on a house you used only as your personal residence. The IRS says Section 1031 does not apply to real property you gave up if it was used solely as your personal residence at the time of the exchange.

A different rule may help. If you owned and used the property as your main home for at least a total of 2 years during the 5-year period ending on the date of the exchange, Section 121 may let you exclude part or all of the gain. The IRS refers readers to Publication 523 for how that exclusion works.

A house used partly as a home and partly for business or investment is split, with two separate Form 8824 worksheets: one for the home part and one for the business or investment part. Rental houses in Texas that were once your home, or the reverse, deserve a tax adviser's review before you sign a contract.

What Texas steps still apply to a 1031 sale?

The federal rule changes how gain is taxed, not how a Texas sale is carried out. The deed still has to be signed and acknowledged before a notary, or sworn before two witnesses, and it is recorded with the county clerk of the county where the property lies.

The Texas property tax calendar also runs on its own track. A tax lien for each year attaches January 1, and a buyer cannot get clear title until delinquent taxes are paid, so a title company will settle any tax owed from the sale funds. Texas has no state property tax, since local governments set rates and collect the money.

  • Gather the legal description early, because the IRS wants real property identified that way or by street address.
  • Ask the county appraisal district and tax office for the tax status of both the old and new property.
  • Keep a copy of the signed identification letter and the date you sent it.

If you are weighing a quick cash sale of an investment house instead, tax treatment differs, so talk to a tax adviser first.

What happens to the deferred gain later?

The gain is deferred, not erased. The IRS Form 8824 instructions say you must file the form with your return for the year you transferred property in a like-kind exchange, and Form 8824 reports the deferred gain or loss.

An exchange with a related party carries a two-year rule. The IRS lists a spouse, child, grandchild, parent, grandparent, brother or sister, and related entities such as certain corporations, partnerships, trusts and estates as related parties. If either side disposes of the property received in such an exchange before the date 2 years after the last transfer, the deferred gain or loss must be reported for the year of the disposition, unless an exception on the form applies. You also file Form 8824 for the two years after a related party exchange.

Frequently asked questions

Does Texas have its own 1031 exchange rules?

The like-kind rule is federal, found in Internal Revenue Code Section 1031. Texas deeds are still recorded with the county clerk, but the like-kind tax treatment comes from federal law.

How long do I have to identify replacement property?

Within 45 days after you transfer the property you give up. The IRS instructions require a signed, clearly described written identification.

How long do I have to close on the replacement property?

By the earlier of 180 days after the transfer or the due date of your tax return, including extensions, for the year of the transfer.

Can I do a 1031 exchange on a house I live in?

No, if it was used solely as your personal residence at the time of the exchange. Section 121 may exclude gain if you owned and used it as your main home for 2 of the last 5 years.

Which form reports a like-kind exchange?

Form 8824, filed with your return for the year of the transfer. The IRS says it is used to report the exchange.

The Federal Housing Finance Agency's purchase-only house price index for Texas stood at 450.76 (not seasonally adjusted) and 444.25 (seasonally adjusted) in the second quarter of 2026, with 1991 Q1 set to 100. The Census Bureau's 2020-2024 estimates put the median value of an owner-occupied Texas home at $283,800.

What do official numbers say about the Texas housing market?

Two federal sources give a clear statewide picture: the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) house price index and Census Bureau QuickFacts. Neither predicts prices, and neither describes one street, so treat them as context for a sale and not as a valuation.

The Census Bureau estimates Texas had 31,709,821 residents on July 1, 2025, up 8.8% from the April 2020 estimates base. It counts 12,848,245 housing units for the same date.

What does the FHFA price index show for Texas?

The FHFA index for Texas stood at 450.76 not seasonally adjusted and 444.25 seasonally adjusted in the second quarter of 2026, with the first quarter of 1991 set to 100. In plain terms, the index says repeat-sale prices in Texas are a little over four and a half times the 1991 starting level.

The index follows price changes in repeated transactions on mortgages that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac bought or guaranteed. It does not report the price of any one house, so it can differ from what a particular neighborhood experienced, and it tracks repeat sales of the same properties over time. The recent quarters are below.

FHFA purchase-only state series for Texas, index with 1991 Q1 = 100

The seasonally adjusted column moves in a narrow band across these six quarters, between 441.17 and 446.73. Read the pattern as a plateau in the series, and ask a local agent or appraiser what your own area did.

What does Census QuickFacts say about Texas homes and owners?

The owner-occupied housing unit rate at 62.6% for 2020 to 2024, and the median value of owner-occupied units at $283,800 for the same period. These are survey-based figures for the whole state.

  • Median selected monthly owner costs, 2020 to 2024: $2,106 with a mortgage and $678 without one.
  • Median gross rent, 2020 to 2024: $1,403.
  • Households, 2020 to 2024: 10,992,816, at 2.69 persons per household.
  • Building permits issued in 2025: 210,217.
  • Median household income, 2020 to 2024 in 2024 dollars: $78,476.

The gap between the $2,106 and $678 owner-cost medians shows how much of ownership cost is the mortgage. Property tax is part of owner costs on both lines, which is why the tax calendar matters to a seller.

Why are there two columns in the index table?

The not seasonally adjusted column reports raw quarterly values, so it swings with the buying season. The seasonally adjusted column smooths out that pattern, which makes quarter to quarter comparison fairer.

Across the six quarters above, the raw column ran from a low of 439.98 in the fourth quarter of 2025 to a high of 450.76 in the second quarter of 2026. Sellers comparing a spring reading with a winter one should use the adjusted column, and anyone quoting the series should name which column they mean.

How fast is Texas growing, and what does that mean for housing?

Texas added about 2.56 million residents between the April 2020 estimates base of 29,149,498 and the July 2025 estimate of 31,709,821. The 2020 census count was 29,145,505, and the 2010 count was 25,145,561.

Housing supply follows people. Builders took out 210,217 building permits in 2025 And the state counts 111.6 people per square mile as of 2020, against 96.3 in 2010. Over 261,000 square miles of land means growth is uneven: a metro suburb and a rural county can sit at opposite ends of the same statewide average.

Who lives in Texas homes?

A few details that shape demand for houses.

  • Persons under 18: 24.0% of the population; persons 65 and over: 14.9%.
  • Veterans, 2020 to 2024: 1,402,357.
  • Living in the same house one year earlier: 86.0% of residents aged one and older.
  • In the civilian labor force: 64.7% of residents aged 16 and over, with a mean commute of 26.7 minutes.
  • Persons in poverty: 13.4%.

The 65-and-older share and the veteran count matter for sellers because both groups can qualify for homestead tax relief, which changes what a buyer inherits in carrying cost. Ask the appraisal district what exemptions are attached to a property before you quote its taxes to a buyer.

Why do median values differ from what homes sell for?

The QuickFacts median is the owners' own estimate of value in a multi-year survey. It lags the market and covers every kind of owner-occupied home, from rural ranch houses to suburban new builds.

The FHFA series is built from transactions, but it is a relative index. It tells you how prices moved against 1991, not what a three-bedroom house is worth today. For a number you can negotiate with, a local comparable sales review or an appraisal does the work that statewide data cannot.

How do property taxes fit into Texas home values?

Property tax is local in Texas, and January 1 is the valuation date. Your bill depends on the value and owner of record that day.

  • Homestead notices of value arrive in spring, so an index reading in the news can be compared with your own notice.
  • A protest to the appraisal review board is the route when your notice looks higher than local sales support.
  • Rates are adopted in the fall, ahead of bills.

A homestead also carries a 10 percent yearly cap on appraised value, which keeps a rising market from passing straight into the taxable base.

What does the Census say about the economy behind Texas housing demand?

Demand for houses rests on jobs and income, and QuickFacts gives several measures for Texas. Per capita income for 2020 to 2024 is $40,752 in 2024 dollars, and the employer count for 2023 was 670,878 establishments with total employment of 12,012,629.

  • Total employment changed by 4.4% between 2022 and 2023.
  • Annual payroll in 2023 was $805,008,752 thousand.
  • Retail sales in 2022 totaled $608,178,719 thousand, or $20,252 per capita.
  • Employer firms in 2023 numbered 470,732, of which 22,721 were veteran-owned.
  • Households with a broadband subscription: 91.4% for 2020 to 2024.
  • High school graduates or higher among adults 25 and older: 86.0%; bachelor's degree or higher: 33.8%.

None of these converts into a home price, but they show a large, working state where the share of households that own is under two thirds.

What should a Texas seller take from the data?

Use the statewide figures for background and rely on local evidence for pricing. The 2026 quarterly index values show a steady series, and the Census medians describe an owner base that is mostly homeowners, but neither can say what a specific house will fetch or how long it will take to close.

Before taking an offer, pull your appraisal notice and ask the county tax office for the current-year payoff. Because the year's lien attaches on January 1, taxes belong in the closing math even if the bill has not been mailed.

What is the FHFA house price index for Texas?

It was 450.76 not seasonally adjusted and 444.25 seasonally adjusted for the second quarter of 2026, with 1991 Q1 equal to 100. It tracks repeat-sale price changes, not any one home.

What is the median home value in Texas?

$283,800 for owner-occupied units in 2020 to 2024, per the Census Bureau. It is a statewide survey median, and local medians differ.

What share of Texans own their homes?

About 62.6%, by the QuickFacts owner-occupied rate for 2020 to 2024.

Can this data predict where Texas prices are heading?

No. Both sources report history, and neither offers a forecast. Use local comparable sales for pricing a particular house.

When do Texas tax bills arrive?

Around October 1, per the Comptroller's pay page. Anything unpaid on February 1 is delinquent, and a bill mailed after January 10 can push that date back.

Texas Property Records: How Deeds and Liens Are Recorded and Found

Cash Home Buyers in Texas

Last updated November 14, 2026.

In Texas, the county clerk serves as the county recorder, and deeds and other instruments are recorded in the county where the property is located. Local Government Code Sec. 191.001 says so, citing Article V, Section 20 of the Texas Constitution. This guide covers what the statutes say about recording.

Title or lien problem?
We buy as-is, including houses with record or lien issues. Tell us what you found.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which office holds the land records for a house in Texas?

The clerk of the county containing the house holds them. In Texas the county clerk doubles as the recorder, and the courts' clerk manual lists that role next to two others: secretary to the commissioners court and filer of probate matters.

A seller living in Dallas with a house in another county therefore deals with the second county's clerk. The Comptroller counts 254 counties, and each runs its own index. Some post searchable images online and others expect a visit, so call the clerk's office before planning a trip.

What kinds of papers end up in the Texas deed records?

Ownership transfers and the paper that surrounds them. The 2023 clerk manual names these deed types: general warranty, special warranty, quitclaim, trustee's, sheriff's and tax. Affidavits, loan releases, leases, sales contracts and powers of attorney sit alongside them.

  • Deeds that pass ownership from one party to another.
  • Deeds of trust that secure a loan, and the releases that end them.
  • Notices of a lender's auction, filed by the clerk ahead of the sale.
  • State tax lien notices from the Comptroller, which the clerk enters in a state tax lien book.
  • Court papers that carry title after a death.

A title search reads all of these in order, which is why a house with a messy record can take longer to close.

What must a deed show to be accepted for filing?

Signature plus acknowledgment, or a sworn statement before two witnesses who sign too. The manual cites Property Code section 12.001(b) and lists notaries, clerks and county court judges among those who can take an acknowledgment.

A deed missing that step may be refused. Leaving out the buyer's mailing address can add a fee. Compare names on the new deed with the name on the last recorded deed, because small differences, such as a dropped middle initial, lead to questions at closing. Title companies and attorneys normally draft the deed so such points get checked first.

What do clerks charge to record a deed?

The base amounts are set by statute and printed in the manual, with county add-ons on top. The table shows the figures from the 2023 edition.

Clerk charges listed in the Texas courts' 2023 county clerk manual
ChargeAmount printed
First page of an instrument$5.00
Each added page, part of a page or attachment$4.00
Each name beyond five that must be indexed$0.25
Records management and preservationNo more than $10
Records archiveNo more than $10
Records technology and infrastructure$2.00
Filing a foreclosure sale notice$2.00 per notice

A commissioners court may direct the clerk to waive real property recording fees for buyers using certain federal or state grant programs. Current schedules sit on the clerk's website or at the counter.

Does Texas add a transfer tax to deed filings?

None appears in the clerk manual or the Comptroller pages, which describe recording charges only. Confirm the full cost list for your closing with the clerk or a title company.

Property tax is its own cost. Each year's tax lien arises at the new year, and the person who owned the house then remains liable even after a sale, as the Comptroller's payment page explains. A closing therefore divides the year's tax between the parties, and a title search checks earlier years for unpaid amounts.

How do liens and sale deeds show up in the records?

Mortgages appear as recorded deeds of trust, and payoff leads to a recorded release. When a lender never filed that release, the old deed of trust can still appear in a search and may need clearing before a sale.

Tax matters leave other marks. The yearly property tax lien arises without any filing, while a state tax lien is a recorded notice. Deeds from tax sales are filed with the clerk too, and the filing date starts the redemption clock. A Texas Supreme Court opinion describes homestead, agricultural and mineral property as redeemable for two years from the filing of the purchaser's deed, with a 25 percent premium in the first year and 50 percent in the second, plus the other costs the opinion lists. Other property follows a shorter 180-day window.

  • Deeds of trust and releases.
  • State tax lien notices.
  • Tax foreclosure deeds and sheriff's deeds.
  • Any judgment or contractor claim that the clerk has indexed.

What shows up in the records after a death or a foreclosure?

After a death, the paper depends on the route taken. The State Law Library pairs an administered estate with an executor's or administrator's deed, a muniment with the court order and will, and a transfer on death deed with an affidavit of death and death certificate. The clerk cannot add heirs to an earlier deed.

A foreclosure leaves its own trail. Lenders post a sale notice at the courthouse and file it with the clerk three weeks or more ahead. The commissioners court designates the sale area and records it. The Attorney General's informal guidance puts sales between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., normally on the month's first Tuesday, and the buyer's trustee deed is recorded afterward like any other deed.

What can a former owner reclaim after a tax or lender sale?

A former owner may have money coming. The State Law Library says a former owner has two years from a tax foreclosure sale to claim any surplus. After a lender's sale, extra funds go to junior lienholders first and then the former owner.

The same guide says a borrower can face a deficiency suit, which must be filed within two years of the sale, and may ask for a fair market value offset. Redemption after a lender's sale exists only for certain kinds, such as owners' association assessment liens. Recorded deeds show the sale date, so the dates in the clerk's records are the starting point for every one of these deadlines.

Someone still living in a house after a sale may face an eviction case, which is a court matter and not a records question. The buyer's deed in the land records is the proof the buyer would show.

How can a seller review the record before listing?

Pull the latest deed and any open deed of trust, then ask a title company or the clerk for a search. Finding a defect early leaves time to fix it.

  • Match the owner's name on the deed to the name used on the listing.
  • Locate the deed of trust and confirm the payoff or release.
  • Ask whether any state tax lien notice is on file.
  • Look up the appraisal district record for owner of record and exemptions.
  • For an inherited house, confirm the probate paper is recorded in the right county.

These steps cost little and often save weeks at the closing table for a Texas seller.

Frequently asked questions

Who maintains Texas land records?

The clerk for the land's county, who acts as recorder for deeds, loan documents, liens and sale notices.

What does filing a deed cost at the clerk's counter?

The manual's 2023 edition shows $5.00 for the opening page and $4.00 for each page after it, plus capped add-ons. The clerk's current schedule gives the total.

What must a Texas deed carry to be recorded?

A signature with an acknowledgment, or a sworn statement before two witnesses. A notary can take the acknowledgment, as can some other officers.

Can a clerk write heirs onto an old deed?

No. A new instrument, such as an executor's deed, muniment order or affidavit of death, has to be recorded.

Where do foreclosure notices go?

The notice must be on the courthouse door and with the clerk 21 days or more before the sale, and the manual lists a $2.00 filing fee. The manual lists a $2.00 fee per notice.
